title: Double default transcript test concurrency
description:
Double the transcript runner's default case concurrency so each logical CPU has two case slots. On a host with 16 logical CPUs, the default rises from 16 to 32; the minimum rises from two to four. Explicit `--jobs N` values keep their existing behavior.

Update the CLI help and development guide, and add a public runner regression that gates four cases on a simulated two-CPU host. This change affects test tooling; application and runtime behavior are unchanged.

title: Refresh integration SDKs and GitHub caches weekly
description:
Follow up #142 by testing Python integrations against current SDK releases after each weekly cache reset, so upstream breaking changes surface in CI. Remove exact SDK test pins while retaining the published dependency minimums and keeping MCP on the supported major with `==2.*`. Satisfying uv environments can be reused between resets.

Scope every enabled GitHub Actions cache and restore prefix to the UTC ISO week: uv, IR/renv, R package libraries, Cargo downloads and build data, source archives, staged runners, and finished wheels. Manual release builds also use a weekly uv cache; tag-driven release builds and publication do not restore uv caches.

Update the test and release documentation to describe weekly CI refreshes and explicit local SDK upgrades. This changes development infrastructure only; the Python API and published dependency constraints are unchanged.

title: Expose launcher retirement races and remove duplicate expectations
description:
The launcher-retirement races repeated native interposer setup, FIFO management, process observation, and cleanup around a short sequence of meaningful events. Give those resources one fixture owner while keeping the two interleavings visible in their test bodies: launcher exit before signal delivery, and launcher exit before the signal call returns.

Remove terminal assertions that repeat the complete result dictionaries in canonical snapshots. Keep checks for readiness, checkpoint order, process identity, and retirement completion, along with raw output checks whose values are normalized before recording.

This changes test organization only. The scenarios, runtime behavior, and transcript snapshots are unchanged.

title: Clarify boundary test imports
description:
## Summary

PR #197 split the boundary tests by behavior, but many split modules retained the old monolith's complete import and constant prelude. Other boundaries also imported standard-library and shared test-support names indirectly through their local harnesses.

This follow-up removes those unused preludes and makes each dependency explicit. None. The test cases, selectors, snapshots, and runtime behavior are unchanged.

## Internal changes

Boundary-local harnesses remain large and are intentionally not redesigned here. The next follow-up will separate fixture control, process helpers, normalization, and MCP support.

title: Test Darwin worker stop and continue supervision
description:
## Summary

Add a macOS public MCP regression for the Darwin behavior where an exit-only wait can still report pending stop or continue notifications. The test stops the relay's direct worker before it execs Zod, then resumes it through explicit process and filesystem gates.

The regression covers startup and evaluation, relay interrupt supervision while the worker is stopped, intentional restart retirement, and a normally evaluating replacement generation.

## User-facing changes

None. This is a tests-only follow-up.

## Internal changes

- Verify the direct worker's stopped state, parent and process group, old-generation retirement, and exact failure cleanup.
- Record the public MCP results for interrupt, restart without a crash diagnostic, and replacement evaluation.

description:

description:

title: Normalize common ANSI sequences in bounded output previews
description:
## Problem

ANSI styling and erase-line controls remained literal in bounded output previews, obscuring useful output from progress redraws. Native diagnostics and worker stderr shared a producer identity, so an unfinished control string could hide another producer's text while the raw log retained its bytes. Three new ANSI test transcripts also nested fixture JSON inside the string-valued `send.r`, making their inputs difficult to read.

## Fix

Add a bounded incremental plain-text projection for SGR styling and common erase-line controls. Suppress control-string payloads and unsupported complete screen operations. Bound CSI parsing and document deterministic recovery for malformed, oversized and incomplete sequences. Reuse the existing frame and output-tape boundaries to preserve CR frame replacement, Unicode-scalar backspace, split UTF-8, finite cuts, delivery recovery, image ordering and the complete 8 KiB text budget. Raw recordings retain exact original bytes.

Give each native diagnostic reader a distinct producer identity so switching between native diagnostics and worker stderr resets incomplete ANSI state. Production changes stay in the terminal projection and its tape integration; the owning runtime document specifies the supported behavior. The public change is preview text projection; producer identity and fixture transport are internal, with no public schema or serializer change.

Public regressions cover arbitrary byte splits, producer switches, polls, images, malformed controls and useful output after heavy redraws. Gated diagnostic cases preserve ingestion ordering and compare exact raw bytes separately. Fixtures own their temporary storage, select known samples/events through named string operations in `send.r`, and record those inputs as separately labeled YAML mappings/lists. The existing precise ONNX diagnostic normalizer accepts plain previews and colored subprocess references while retaining other diagnostics.

## Validation

title: Fix control-only interrupt while another send owns evaluation polling
description:
## Problem

Console requires code-bearing calls to be sequential, but its [existing tool contract](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/b0c6239139612375fb90f3669abf139163715165/src/server.rs#L125-L135) explicitly allows a code-free interrupt to overlap a pending `send`.

In that supported overlap, the interrupt signal was already sent successfully. The subsequent attempt to observe the evaluation could fail with `worker evaluation is already being polled`, because the original send still owned polling. If execution completed during the interrupt, control could also reserve delivery still owned by the original send.

This is not the ordinary sequential `send → running response → interrupt` flow, nor does it require two cells executing concurrently. It requires two requests overlapping at the server. An asynchronous client can do this directly. Another possible path is a harness locally abandoning a waiting call, then issuing an interrupt on a later turn while the earlier server request remains outstanding. Codex source inspection suggests that path is possible, but it has **not** been reproduced end to end. A generic Stop action is not itself Console's `send(control="interrupt")`.

## Fix

Keep interrupt signaling separate from ownership of the original send's output. Under the existing evaluation-state mutex, collect the result only if the interrupt can claim observation. Otherwise return a successful running response and leave polling and delivery with the original send.

Use the same rule during startup and completion. This changes the previously tested polling-error response for overlapping interrupts; it does not add concurrent cell execution or claim to fix failed signal delivery. Deterministic regressions cover active polling, completion during interrupt handling, retained text/image output, and subsequent cell execution.

## Validation

Committed the two-file repair as `5c5d15c6`; `scripts/check` passed on that clean revision. `scripts/preflight`, unchanged `scripts/format`, and `git diff --check` passed. The identical committed content passed 22 cases / 44 direct and sandboxed executions with:

```sh
scripts/test --jobs 4 client_server/lifecycle/test_interrupts client_server/lifecycle/test_control_polling server_relay/interrupts/test_interrupts client_server/python/test_without_r::automatic_resolution_failure_and_cancel_keep_accepted_state client_server/requirements/test_python_automatic_lifecycle::interrupts_automatic_python_resolver_and_preserves_worker client_server/requirements/test_python_automatic_lifecycle::interrupts_no_r_automatic_python_resolver_and_preserves_worker
```

Both ownership regressions failed before the implementation fix. The stopped-worker assertion failed before this repair; its snapshot was regenerated using `scripts/test --update client_server/lifecycle/test_interrupts::supervises_stopped_and_continued_workers`. Validation ran on macOS arm64. Linux and Windows were not run; Docker, SBX, and external SSH were unavailable. Hosted CI on this head passed Windows and Ubuntu but failed macOS in `invalid_probe_results_retire_before_worker_startup` with a truncated prepared-probe frame. The failure remains unexplained; passing focused reruns does not establish a fix. [CI run](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/actions/runs/37215996070).

title: Keep Python’s main namespace clean and minimize Console-specific names
description:
## Problem

## Fix

The fresh-session transcript starts with exactly print(globals()) and its full seven-key Python 3.13 output. The following False True observation shows that _console is a builtin and is absent from globals(). Existing Python r and R bridge conveniences remain documented intentional entry points.

Consolidate coverage into four cases: fresh namespace/builtin location with one restart; bridge callbacks, pickle identity and deliberate rebindings; interrupted setup preserving startup bindings; and activation errors propagated to R. Existing bridge, lifecycle, peer-runtime and SQL tests cover the removed order/restart duplication.

Changed-file count falls from 14 to 12, and added lines from 1,402 to 691. Transcript volume falls from six snapshots/935 lines to four/301 lines (68% fewer lines). title: Simplify SQL connection helper names
description:
Passing an open R connection to `sql_connection(reader@con)` fails with an unused-argument error because getting and selecting SQL connections use different helpers. The R getter can also return an inactive connection while SQL cells use Python.

Replace both top-level helpers with `.console$sql_connection()` in R and `_console.sql_connection()` in Python, without compatibility aliases. Omission returns the active native connection, a supplied connection selects it, and `NULL`/`None` restores the same managed connection and catalog without closing user connections. Getters report ownership by the other runtime. Reset does not replay captured startup; restart creates a new worker generation.

Internally, inspection of existing adapter state keeps getters consistent with SQL routing. Migrate runtime consumers, startup fixtures and examples, tool guidance, documentation, and generated public snapshots. Public regressions cover native identity, transactions, reset, restart, and hidden SQL providers.

title: Unify DuckDB default extensions
description:
## Problem

Managed DuckDB declared icu/json/sqlite defaults with R and only sqlite without R, so inspection and reset reported different defaults despite Python builds often including ICU and JSON. The defaults fixture also assumed startup had finished before inspecting requirements.

## Fix

Share one canonical default list across managed providers, reusing existing built-in detection and preparation. Preserve empty Windows defaults and the previous non-Windows compile boundary. Consolidate public R/no-R coverage for JSON extraction, exact timezone results and read-only SQLite attachment with automatic installation disabled. Verify fresh SQLite preparation without ICU/JSON downloads, wait for public readiness before inventory inspection, retain meaningful non-default extension-addition tests, and update documentation and generated inventories. Explicit set/reset and user-owned connections retain their behavior.

## Validation

title: Retry runtime discovery after setup repair
description:
## Problem

Failed runtime discovery or initial preparation remained cached after setup was repaired, requiring a new server. Retrying must preserve accepted environments and cells while preventing duplicate discovery attempts and replay of rejected work.

## Fix

Explicit `control="restart"` retries failed initial setup under the connection's existing owner, using captured trusted configuration and current filesystem/tool availability. Concurrent restart callers share one attempt. Ordinary sends retain the latest diagnostic, and tool discovery keeps its stable schema.

Each cell retains its admitted readiness attempt. Rejected code, stdin and requirements are never replayed. Retry requires confirmed preparation retirement, including protocol closure, child reaping and I/O settlement. Request cancellation leaves shared preparation running; connection closure cancels and retires it. Cancellation before payload admission withholds code or stdin while preserving accepted environments and usable prepared workers.

Code-free retries route stdin through accepted evaluations under ordinary polling ownership. Changed requirements start the prepared replacement. Failed discovery and subsequent preparation, startup and idle output share the original session log. Shutdown retains completed setup and cleanup failures. Post-acceptance worker recovery remains separate.

Internal readiness, admission, preparation retirement and recording changes have corresponding documentation and public regressions. No-R retry fixtures now use `without_r()` before selecting Python, preventing inherited `R_HOME` from diverting them into R startup.

## Validation

Reproduced all three affected public-case failures with a valid inherited `R_HOME`. After repair, the startup-retry suite passed with that same setting: 15 cases / 26 executions, including direct and sandboxed sessions. Assertions and snapshots were unchanged.

title: Expose latest status for Console-owned startup and preparation phases
description:
A caller polling `send` currently sees `[worker starting]` or `[running; poll with an empty send]` whether Console is discovering runtimes, preparing dependencies, or replacing a worker. The response gives no indication of which Console operation is still pending. This is especially confusing after an interrupt or a cancelled poll: the request can finish while the underlying operation still needs to settle.

This PR includes the current Console-owned phase in applicable responses: `startup`, `dependency preparation`, or `replacement`. For an admitted cell, the phase appears in its elapsed notice, for example `[elapsed: 2.3s since admission; phase: dependency preparation]`. Background startup without an admitted cell uses a separate `[phase: startup]` notice and has no cell clock. Public tools and arguments are unchanged.

Internally, disposable observations read the existing operation owners without blocking a response. They are tied to the relevant generation and operation, remain valid until completion or retirement, and keep worker startup visible through transport readiness. Completed observations fall through to current lifecycle work, replacement remains visible until its single successor reaches transport readiness, and recovered responses refresh their observation when a current owner is available. A busy evaluation observation is omitted; completion allows the lifecycle fallback. Retirement is confirmed before a replacement worker starts. Interrupt submission and poll cancellation do not falsely mark unfinished work complete.

Phase text shares the existing 8 KiB response budget and does not accumulate in retained output or alter admission, environment commits, response recovery, or cleanup. Ephemeral phase projections share retained image content to avoid an additional full-image copy.

The change also updates public response fixtures, the R client's readiness handling, and the `send` contract for phase-bearing responses. Public regressions cover phase transitions, completion and retirement, response recovery, output budgets, and image allocation.

Reset preserves the managed catalog and user connections. R previews use a separate scratch catalog.

title: Separate target stop reasons from I/O cancellation and cleanup evidence
description:
## Problem

During target capture and probe, interrupt and shutdown shared an I/O wake token. A failed cancellation check could turn a poll failure into requested cancellation, while the token could not establish cleanup. Setup could also hide workload, I/O or owner-exit failures during shutdown or after a valid provider retirement receipt.

## Fix

Retain the first accepted control cause for the complete setup operation, with command admission and completion under the same lock. Use a separate command abort token for I/O failures so provider cleanup commands remain admissible. Settle each child, exit observer and I/O task before publishing a setup report, preserving captured protocol bytes even when the command fails.

Parse provider retirement evidence independently from the command result. Before provider launch, confirmation covers local retirement; after launch, require the existing generation receipt. Preserve independent workload, infrastructure and abnormal owner-exit failures alongside cleanup evidence. Startup suppresses only confirmed connection shutdown or a clean next-stage registration refusal, retaining preparation-close failures and the refused stage's handle.

Document these ownership rules and cover them through public MCP/CLI tests with causal admission, control and receipt gates. Gate prepared startup prompts before collecting output. R/Python exceptions and sideband shape, generation identity, provider replacement policies and native retirement authority remain unchanged.

title: Separate cell admission from worker receipts and response delivery
description:
## Problem

Serialize bootstrap receipts, interrupt admission and Evaluate enqueue under short controller guards, releasing them before acknowledgment waits and pipe I/O. Settle execution from terminal receipts or generation failure independently of response collection and delivery.

Retain one interrupt selection across resolver preparation, startup admission and established connections. Preserve replacement identity, outstanding idle input, lazy startup failure output, the ordinary cell slot, acknowledgment ordering and the observation grace. title: Converge generation shutdown on one idempotent retirement owner
description:
## Problem

Restart racing EOF could send Shutdown twice because startup, restart, failed-worker recovery and connection shutdown used separate retirement paths. Later observers could lose retirement I/O failures or the failed worker's exit outcome, and EOF cancellation could suppress a genuine setup failure. Multistage preparation could attach an earlier stage's control to a later independent failure. Failed-worker teardown also held the lifecycle mutex across callbacks and joins; the suspected deadlock was not reproduced.

## Fix

Each worker launch now owns one retained retirement operation. Lifecycle reserves the original budgets under its mutex, then releases it before command writes, resolver cancellation, process waits and task joins. Startup failure, restart, EOF and failed-worker recovery share one Shutdown request and terminal result. Late startup registration retires before startup completes, and failed-worker transitions verify generation identity after teardown. Launcher retirement and defensive Drop share the existing resource owner's cleanup path.

Retirement keeps normal command/barrier evidence separate from physical cleanup and I/O settlement. Confirmed reaping and successful I/O settlement can supersede a failed normal barrier while preserving independent cleanup errors. Replacement requires confirmed owned resources and successful I/O. Concurrent restart preserves the retiring generation's exit outcome and output ownership.

Startup cancellation uses the server's original shutdown deadline and consumes the preparation owner's retained terminal report. Control consumed after collection retains its cause before publication. Multistage preparation takes control only from a subprocess report matching the final result; cleanup confirmation includes every stage.

Public changes remove duplicate shutdown diagnostics and preserve failure evidence and replacement barriers. Internal changes consolidate retirement and task ownership, removing duplicate startup-cancellation, task-cleanup, Drop and allowance-handoff paths. Original allowances, dispatcher-observation policy, R initialization, protocol versions and response delivery are preserved. Production changes total +490/-267 lines, net +223. The architecture documents the ownership contract.

## Validation

title: Make server-to-relay command writes independently cancellable
description:
## Problem

Queued Stop could not interrupt target bootstrap or a blocked JSONL command write. Retirement used stdout closure to decide whether to join the stdin writer, although descendants can retain these streams independently. Public regressions reproduced blocked retirement and missing writer joins. Aborted partial frames and a relay-exit/admission race also prevented replacement after confirmed cleanup.

## Fix

Give each generation one independently abortable serialization owner and shared terminal admission state. Unix uses cancellable nonblocking writes; Windows uses a dedicated overlapped-I/O cancellation event. Normal retirement preserves ordered Shutdown and grace. Forced retirement closes admission, wakes blocked or idle writers, settles outstanding controls, and joins owned transport tasks. Remove stdout-based writer-retirement decisions and branches that discarded join handles, preserving bounded output drainage and launcher/provider cleanup barriers.

Record relay-exit failure before closing admission. Recognize partial-command EOF caused by local retirement abort without suppressing other fatal or cleanup failures. Add causal public regressions for blocked bootstrap, full command pipes, independently retained streams, repeated restarts, outstanding and late interrupts, partial-frame restart, and SIGKILL during dispatch without replay. Synchronize affected startup fixtures and Windows input completion checks. Include `<stdbool.h>` explicitly for Linux C11 fixture compilation and document writer ownership. Send ordering, observation deadlines and wire shapes remain unchanged.

## Validation

title: Share incremental JSONL framing across Unix and Windows

- `scripts/with-checkout rustc --edition=2024 --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc --emit=metadata tests/fixtures/windows_worker.rs -o /tmp/oss112-refill-holder-windows-worker.rmeta`

The existing native inherited-writer regression skipped on macOS. Native Windows/Linux execution and Windows production compilation remain unverified; metadata compilation checks fixture types only. The cancellation-plus-queued-suffix retirement transition is not independently forced by a checkpoint. The portable framing baseline passed before the refactor; this repair has no native Windows red/green result.

Passed local checks: `uv run --no-project --python 3.13 python scripts/check`.

title: Consolidate native direct-child exit observation
description:
## Problem

Relay and resolver owners duplicated native non-reaping exit observation. Windows notifications discarded wait failures, and shutdown could reap before observation settled. Windows retirement tests also reopened PIDs after completion, when [PID identity is no longer guaranteed](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/procthread/process-handles-and-identifiers).

## Fix

Centralize platform selection and native observation under process_exit. Migrated consumers receive explicit exit/error results and settle observation before their sole reapers. Preserve Unix WNOWAIT, PID validation, EINTR retries and Darwin stop/continue handling. Windows observation shares the existing resolver retirement deadline while retaining separate empty-Job confirmation. Failed relay status observation still attempts termination. Public regressions use causal checkpoints, fixtures retire owned groups, and Windows acceptance pins original process handles before acknowledging readiness. Protocols and termination/retirement owners remain unchanged.

## Validation

Committed repair b41affe1. On that clean revision, all six focused resolver/relay cases and scripts/check passed. Preflight, unchanged formatting and git diff --check passed. The real fixture acknowledgment diagnostic failed before the change and passed afterward. WORKPAD.md records evidence and disposition. Native Windows/.cmd and Linux execution are unavailable locally; hosted Windows must rerun. PID reuse in the earlier failure remains unconfirmed.

Passed local checks: `uv run --no-project --python 3.13 python scripts/check`.

title: Retire standalone sandbox processes after launcher loss
description:
## Summary

Make `mcp-console sandbox` retire its process tree and clean up or preserve its private temporary directory after abrupt launcher loss. This extends the crash-manager ownership model used by worker generations while keeping normal standalone status and cleanup ownership in the launcher.

## User-facing changes

- A standalone target cannot start until the launcher tracker is attached and the manager has adopted the temporary directory and reported readiness. A private inherited descriptor releases the target wrapper, which then closes the descriptor and executes the requested command in the same process.
- Abrupt launcher loss retires the exact observed root and descendant identities, including descendants that start another session. Successful crash cleanup also removes the private temporary directory.
- If the manager exits unexpectedly, the launcher wakes from its process wait and performs local retirement. A failed manager recovery signal now returns a bounded error and preserves the temporary directory instead of leaving the launcher blocked.
- A manager cleanup acknowledgement timeout selects preservation in both the manager and the owner, even if the manager subsequently exits normally. Ordinary cleanup still removes the directory and preserves the target exit status.
- Executable names that look like command options remain accepted after the private target-wrapper handoff.

## Internal changes

- The launcher continues to own normal observation, retirement, direct-child status, and final directory disposition. The manager supplies independent crash recovery and participates only in the bounded retirement handoff.
- Recovery targets exact PID and start-time identities. It does not signal an unpinned process group.
- An explicit manager-monitor wakeup interrupts the standalone tracker's blocking wait when manager recovery completes or fails.
- Cleanup preparation now distinguishes completion, timeout, and control failure so owner-side directory cleanup follows the selected disposition without changing successful manager-crash recovery.
- The `sandbox-exec` command explicitly removes host `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES`, so loader interposers do not cross into the Apple intermediary or sandbox target when platform filtering is absent.
- Public macOS CLI transcripts use causal descriptor and FIFO checkpoints to cover startup adoption, failed manager recovery, cleanup timeout, and launcher loss during retirement.

## Intentional limits

- Darwin cannot atomically attach either post-spawn observer. A descendant that becomes orphaned before an observer sees it remains outside that observer's guarantee.
- Abrupt launcher loss before manager readiness is not covered.
- Temporary-directory removal remains best effort when sandbox contents make removal impossible.
- This change does not add terminal job control or signal forwarding.

## Notes

Local validation covered `scripts/format`, `scripts/check-core`, the complete transcript suite serially with Python 3.12, and the complete standalone crash-recovery suite. An ad-hoc arm64e executable reproduced the hosted runner's loader mismatch before the platform-boundary fix. The exact six-worker transcript command reached the unrelated `client_server/zod::supervises_stopped_and_continued_workers` lifecycle assertion; that case passed when rerun serially.

title: Route SQL cells to Python DB-API connections
description:
## Summary

Route SQL cells directly to Python-owned DB-API connections alongside the existing R-owned DBI provider. This lets callers use Python database drivers without converting connection or result objects through reticulate, while preserving managed DuckDB as the default provider and retaining its R-workspace integration.

## User-facing changes

- Install `console_sql_connection(connection)` in Python. Passing `None` requests restoration of managed DuckDB for the next SQL cell.
- Use the most recent R or Python selection for later SQL cells. An R selection clears the Python provider.
- Retain the exact Python connection. Execute directly on connections that expose `execute()` so DuckDB connection-local state persists; otherwise use the standard DB-API cursor protocol.
- Apply the bounded SQL-preview contract to Python results: at most 20 rows and 12 columns, 160-character cells, 200 display columns, and 12 KiB total output.
- Keep selected Python connections reusable after database errors, interrupts, and exceptions raised during execution or cursor cleanup.
- Do not start automatic Python package resolution from SQL driver calls. Prepare driver dependencies with `requirements.python` or import them from a Python cell.

## Internal changes

- Extend the existing Rust-owned CPython facade to install and call the embedded DB-API adapter, keeping one retained `libpython` handle and one initialization policy.
- Keep provider selection and connection objects in their owning runtimes. Managed DuckDB restoration remains lazy inside the existing R SQL error boundary.
- Consolidate Python provider selection and evaluation into one CPython dispatch boundary. The complete driver, preview, and cleanup call runs with automatic import resolution suspended, while escaping Python exceptions remain ordinary cell output.
- Update runtime-source validation, tool schemas, public documentation, transcript coverage, and generated goldens.

## Limitations

- R's `sql_connection()` remains R-owned and does not proxy a Python connection.
- `requirements.duckdb` prepares only managed R-backed DuckDB. Python drivers and their dependencies use `requirements.python`.
- Selected drivers remain responsible for SQL dialect, transaction, and type behavior. Previews do not report affected-row or total-result counts.

title: Retire observed descendants with each worker generation
description:
## Summary

Retire descendants observed from each sandboxed relay when its worker generation ends through explicit restart, automatic replacement, or orderly server shutdown. Without generation-owned cleanup, a processx-style descendant that moved to another process group or session could survive after the worker-generation cleanup returned.

## User-facing changes

- Restart, failure replacement, and shutdown now wait for observed descendants across process-group and session changes to stop.
- A generation's private temporary directory is removed only after successful retirement and is preserved when cleanup reports an error.
- MCP tool shapes, worker behavior, and the relay descriptor boundary are unchanged.

## Internal changes

- `SandboxedChild` owns a continuously serviced PID/start-time tracker for the relay generation.
- The observer blocks in `kevent()` and uses an `EVFILT_USER` event for lifecycle wakeup. The one-second deadline is reserved for stale-identity maintenance; stop no longer wakes the observer through a 10 ms polling loop.
- The wake handle shares ownership of the kqueue descriptor so an early observer exit cannot turn a later wakeup into a write to a reused descriptor. A wake error remains bounded by the maintenance deadline and is reported with any observation or retirement error.
- Retirement stops the observed tree, closes the original relay process group as a fork-race backstop, and then reaps the direct relay.
- Public transcripts cover restart, failure replacement, and shutdown with a processx child outside the worker session. Existing fallback coverage still exercises a late process-group member.

## Notes

Darwin cannot install the observer atomically with process creation. A descendant that becomes orphaned before the initial root watch or before its fork event is resolved remains outside the guarantee. Cleanup after failure of the server process itself also remains separate work.

Local verification completed with `scripts/check`, the focused lifecycle and fallback transcript cases, and eight concurrent runs of the three-case generation-lifecycle suite.

title: Retire observed descendants after standalone command exit
description:
## Summary

The standalone macOS `mcp-console sandbox` command previously returned when its direct command exited, even when observed descendants remained alive in another process group or session. This PR retires that observed process tree before returning, so processx-style background work does not outlive the standalone sandbox lifetime.

## User-facing behavior

- Observe the direct command and its descendants with kqueue and libproc, retaining each process's PID and start time.
- After the direct command exits, complete a signal pass for every observed identity and then allow a one-second reaping grace.
- Preserve the direct command's exit status and remove its private temporary directory after successful retirement.
- If tracker setup or observation fails, retire every identity captured so far and preserve the temporary directory when unknown live work may still use it.

The public transcript coverage exercises nested processx descendants in separate sessions, a processx crash supervisor outside the root process group, inherited ignored `SIGCHLD`, exit-status preservation, and temporary-directory removal.

## Internal changes

- Split process identity, tree discovery, kqueue event tracking, and retirement into modules with those current responsibilities.
- Bound direct-child cleanup after tracker failures and retain partial tracker state for best-effort retirement.
- Remove the unused private normal-wait path from `SandboxedChild`.
- Make transcript failure cleanup compare PID and start time before signaling, retain partially captured identities, and avoid loading macOS libproc before platform selection.

## Limits

Darwin cannot atomically install a descendant observer at spawn time. A descendant that becomes orphaned before the post-spawn root watch or corresponding fork observation remains outside this guarantee. Termination or failure of the launcher itself is also outside this PR's scope.

macOS has no pidfd-style signal API. A PID/start-time check prevents targeting a PID that is already known to have been reused, but a narrow check-to-signal reuse race remains. Discovery and complete signal passes scale with the number of observed processes; the one-second bound is the reaping grace after the first complete pass, not a total cleanup wall-clock limit.

The server/relay worker-generation lifecycle and generic `SandboxedCommand::spawn()` callers are unchanged.

## Testing

- `scripts/check`
- `scripts/test cli/sandbox_supervision`
- Non-Darwin suite-load probe with libproc loading blocked

title: Simplify sandbox manager monitoring and process tracking
description:
## Summary

Simplify macOS sandbox supervision by removing redundant manager waiting and process-tracker state. This makes the existing lifecycle invariants explicit and removes 82 net lines of production Rust without changing the documented cleanup behavior.

## User-facing changes

There are no intentional user-facing behavior changes.

## Internal changes

- Reap the sandbox manager directly with `Child::wait()` and remove the separate blocking `waitid()` wrapper and duplicate stop/reap path.
- Replace the recovery mutex with an `AtomicBool` claim between fallback recovery and cancellation. If recovery claims the root first, the owner still joins that bounded cleanup before releasing the root PID pin.
- Store the tracker's required root identity directly instead of wrapping it in `Option`.
- Remove the stale-process sweep before signaling while retaining identity validation for every signal and reconciliation afterward.
- Add deterministic CLI coverage for a reused descendant PID and for a descendant exiting immediately before the manager signal.

title: Use manager readiness as the sandbox startup barrier
description:
## Summary

Use sandbox manager readiness as the complete startup barrier. The manager now installs root, descendant, and control-socket observation and adopts the private directory before sending `READY`. The owner can therefore install manager-failure recovery and release the gated root without a `COMMIT` / `COMMITTED` round trip.

This removes the ready-but-not-committed state while preserving the startup gate, process identity checks, manager-failure recovery, and directory ownership rules.

## User-facing changes

There are no intended user-facing behavior changes. Built-in relays, configured relays, and standalone commands remain gated until manager supervision is ready and owner-side failure recovery is installed.

## Internal changes

- Remove the commit protocol bytes, the owner-side `commit()` call, and their startup failure branches.
- Register the manager control socket with the manager's `kqueue` before sending `READY`; after readiness, the socket carries no messages and remains only an ownership token.
- Keep manager-failure monitoring before gate release in both managed and standalone startup paths.
- Add deterministic acceptance coverage proving that standalone targets and configured relays start after `READY` without another manager response.
- Retarget the startup-crash regressions to the period after readiness and before gate release, and update the supervision documentation.

## Validation

- `scripts/test --update`
- `scripts/check`

title: Consolidate sandbox child retirement
description:
## Summary

Sandbox child cleanup was implemented separately in worker startup, child retirement, and standalone launcher error paths. This change centralizes those mechanics in `sandbox::child` so all three paths keep the direct root waitable while signaling and reaping it.

The retirement state is reduced to managed, unmanaged, and retired. An unmanaged child remains retryable, and a child only becomes retired once its PID identity has been released. This lets a later shutdown ownership pass retry a transient reap failure.

## User-facing changes

- No changes to successful sandbox execution or normal shutdown.
- In the combined manager-control and reap failure path, later shutdown ownership now retries the reap while preserving the original failure diagnostic.

## Internal changes

- Reuse one bounded unmanaged-child cleanup helper for worker startup and relay retirement.
- Move the standalone root cleanup helper without changing its raw process-group signal or diagnostic behavior.
- Remove duplicate cleanup code and an ignored crate-private doctest.
- Add a deterministic public transcript that injects manager-control and first-reap failures, then verifies retry and complete process cleanup.

## Testing

- Focused sandbox, crash, supervision, startup, and Zod lifecycle transcripts.
- `scripts/check`

title: Cancel blocked relay sideband writes during retirement
description:
## Summary

Keep relay retirement within the worker deadline when the worker-side sideband peer remains open but no longer reads. The relay now retains a cancellation handle and shuts down only its local write half before joining the writer thread. Its read half remains available long enough to forward every complete buffered or immediately readable worker frame.

## User-facing changes

- Server shutdown and worker replacement no longer need the outer relay-retirement fallback to interrupt a sideband writer blocked behind a retained peer socket.
- Worker-sideband messages and output behavior are unchanged.

## Internal changes

- Add an explicit write-half shutdown operation to the sideband writer and retain a cloned endpoint for cancellation.
- Extend the public shutdown regression with a detached fixture process that keeps the worker-side socket open after the direct worker is retired.
- Publish the fixture PID atomically so the test cannot observe a partially written marker, and clean up the detached process explicitly.
- Document write-side cancellation and read-side draining in the relay retirement contract.

## Scope

A worker descendant that leaves the relay process group remains unsupported. This change does not track or stop that process; it only prevents its retained sideband endpoint from pinning the relay writer. It does not change dependencies, generated artifacts, transcript output, or goldens.

## Testing

- `scripts/check`
- `scripts/test --jobs 1 client_server/zod::shutdown_deadline_does_not_wait_for_sideband_writer client_server/zod::shutdown_cancels_partial_sideband_frame client_server/zod::restart_cancels_partial_sideband_frame client_server/zod::restart_drains_readable_frame_before_abandoning_partial_tail`
- Confirmed that the focused regression fails with write-half cancellation removed and passes with the final implementation.
- `ruff format --check tests/fixtures/zod tests/transcripts/client_server/zod.py`
- `git diff --check`

title: Close unlisted inherited descriptors at the relay boundary
description:
## Summary

Prevent unlisted file descriptors inherited by `mcp-console serve` from crossing the server-to-relay boundary. Submitted code should not be able to access unrelated host descriptors, regardless of whether a session uses the built-in components or custom relay and worker executables.

Every relay launch now applies the same post-fork descriptor policy: descriptors above standard error are marked close-on-exec before `sandbox-exec` starts. The relay protocol remains fd 0 for commands, fd 1 for events, and fd 2 for diagnostics.

## User-facing changes

- Unrelated inheritable server descriptors no longer reach the relay or worker in the default, custom-worker, or custom-relay configurations.
- MCP requests, responses, console output, and configuration flags are unchanged.

## Internal changes

- Scan child descriptor slots after fork so descriptors opened by another server thread cannot race a parent-side snapshot.
- Preserve Rust's private exec-error pipe by setting `FD_CLOEXEC` instead of closing descriptors before exec.
- Replace inherited Zod test-control descriptors with FIFO channels created inside the worker's private temporary directory, including a causal response-ordering gate.
- Add public regressions for the default, custom-worker, and custom-relay paths, including an inherited fd 64 above a lowered soft descriptor limit.
- Document the unconditional server-to-relay descriptor boundary.

## Additional notes

The implementation remains macOS-only, matching the project's current platform support. Local validation completed with `scripts/format` and the complete `scripts/check`; the response-ordering regression also passed 50 consecutive runs.

title: Close unlisted file descriptors in the standalone sandbox
description:
## Summary

Prevent standalone `mcp-console sandbox` targets from inheriting unintended file descriptors above standard error. The launcher retains standard input, output, and error while closing other inherited host capabilities before the target runs.

## User-facing changes

- Standalone sandbox commands no longer receive unlisted inherited file descriptors.
- The README documents the standard-stream inheritance boundary.
- A public transcript passes a writable host file as descriptor 64, lowers the launcher's soft descriptor limit below that number, requires the target to observe `EBADF`, and verifies that the host file remains unchanged.

## Internal changes

- Snapshot the standalone launcher's open descriptors in the parent, then set `FD_CLOEXEC` in the child-side pre-exec hook. This leaves the parent's descriptor flags unchanged and preserves Rust's exec-error reporting.
- Scale launch work with the number of open descriptors instead of probing every slot up to the process limit.
- Keep the helper beside the current sandbox implementation instead of placing it in a planned supervision layout.

## Scope and validation

The generic server-to-relay spawn path remains unchanged because development and test workers may receive explicit extra descriptor capabilities; closing those safely requires an allowlist. This PR does not change descendant supervision, process groups, terminal job control, crash recovery, temporary-directory ownership, or server and relay lifecycle behavior.

The public regression was confirmed failing before the implementation and passing afterward. Local validation passed with `RUST_TEST_THREADS=6 scripts/check-core`, `scripts/test --jobs 6`, and the focused `scripts/test cli/sandbox_descriptors` selector. A manual inherited-descriptor probe at fd 200000 also passed.

title: Keep process-group cleanup inside the sandbox launcher
description:
The relay still required itself to be the sandbox process-group leader. An ordinary wrapper could start and use it, but MCP restart then failed with “worker relay is not its process-group leader.” Let the sandbox launcher own process-group and descendant cleanup, while the relay retains direct-worker termination, reaping, and stream drainage. Direct and wrapped relay launches now use the same protocol without requiring a particular process-group identity.

Move the remaining process-group implementation under `src/sandbox` and remove its relay-only branches, reducing production code by 41 lines. Simplify the relay protocol documentation around the process boundary and keep sandbox setup, cleanup, and recovery details in the sandbox documentation. Future sandbox-specific control channels terminate at the launcher. `serve` continues to use the bundled sandbox for every worker generation.

Add regressions comparing direct and sandboxed relay transcripts, exercising MCP restart and shutdown below a wrapper with a descendant retaining worker streams, and checking sandbox setup failure and retry through MCP. The direct and wrapped relay cases failed against the original implementation before the cleanup change.

`scripts/check` passed. The first full run stopped at a managed-Python preparation assertion; that case passed in isolation and in the complete rerun without a behavior change.

title: Unify managed sandbox root startup
description:
## Summary

Give worker generations and `mcp-console sandbox` one managed-root startup transaction. This removes parallel ownership of startup ordering and cleanup so the two launch paths cannot drift while preserving the existing supervision contract.

## User-facing changes

There are no intentional user-facing behavior changes. Worker relays and standalone commands still remain gated until manager observation, directory ownership, and manager-failure recovery are ready. Standalone terminal and signal behavior is unchanged.

## Internal changes

- Add `ManagedRoot::start` as the shared owner of root process setup, manager startup, temporary-directory handoff, gate release, and startup failure cleanup.
- Make the startup gate and supervisor required `ManagedRoot` state, removing the separate direct command constructor and manual standalone gate setup.
- Carry worker and standalone differences through concrete start options for descriptor handling, signal state, terminal ownership, and cleanup timeouts.
- Replace separate worker and standalone manager-start wrappers with one entry point.

## Validation

- `scripts/format`
- `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test --all-targets --all-features`
- Focused public startup, descriptor-boundary, CLI supervision, and manager-crash transcript tests
- A causal PTY replay where the standalone root exits before manager readiness; it preserved exit status 130 and cleaned up the root, manager, and private directory

`scripts/check` reached the full transcript suite. Its only reported failures were three Python multiprocessing/joblib cases where the host could not allocate POSIX semaphores (`OSError: [Errno 28] No space left on device`).

title: Start gated roots before sandbox managers
description:
## Summary

Start each gated sandbox root before its manager. Because the root cannot execute past its startup gate, the manager can now receive the complete startup state as native command arguments without weakening supervision.

This removes the custom initialization frame and collapses manager spawn, readiness, directory ownership transfer, and failure-monitor setup into one constructor that returns a usable manager.

## User-facing changes

There are no intended user-facing changes. Built-in relays, configured relays, and standalone commands remain blocked until manager observation and owner-side recovery are active. Standalone manager processes retain their inherited signal behavior.

## Internal changes

- Pass the root PID, cleanup timeout, and private path through the hidden manager command, and derive the owner PID with `getppid()`.
- Delete the `MCG4` codec and the manager's pre-observation states.
- Keep the owner directory guard until failure monitoring is installed, then release the root gate.
- Add causal startup-order coverage and monitor-creation failure coverage.

title: Run sandbox manager supervision in one event loop
description:
## Summary

Run sandbox-manager process supervision and owner-control observation through one `kqueue` on the manager's sole thread. This removes manager-internal lifecycle coordination that duplicated state already serialized by the event queue.

## User-facing changes

There are no intended user-facing behavior changes. The startup gate and commit exchange remain intact, owner EOF still requests retirement, and cleanup success still controls temporary-directory removal.

## Internal changes

- Register the owner control descriptor beside root and descendant process watches, and retain coalesced root-exit and control-readability facts from each event batch.
- Preserve the separate natural-root-exit and live-root owner-loss cleanup ordering, including waiting for owner EOF after clean natural-exit cleanup.
- Remove the cloned control socket, tracker thread, user-event wakeup, join paths, and mutex-backed process-group backstop arbitration.
- Replace thread-join crash-test gates with deterministic process-group cleanup checkpoints, and remove the test for the deleted tracker-thread startup phase.

## Validation

- `scripts/test --jobs 1 cli/cleanup/test_cleanup cli/crashes/test_crashes cli/recovery/test_recovery cli/signals/test_signals cli/startup/test_startup client_server/sandbox/test_crashes`
- `scripts/check`

## Notes

This is rebased on `ef82946d`, which reorganized the Python boundary suites. It retains the documented boundary that a descendant orphaned before its fork event can be resolved is outside tracked cleanup.

title: Use the manager control socket as an ownership token
description:
## Summary

Treat the committed sandbox-manager control socket as the sandbox lifetime's ownership token. Closing the socket now requests retirement, and the manager uses its own cleanup result to decide whether to remove the private temporary directory.

This removes the post-startup message exchange that duplicated state across the owner, manager, and standalone launcher.

## User-facing changes

- Preserve existing restart, replacement, shutdown, and direct-command cleanup behavior.
- Remove the private temporary directory after successful cleanup even if the standalone launcher exits while retirement is finishing.
- Continue to preserve the directory when manager cleanup fails or times out.

## Internal changes

- Keep the existing readiness and ownership-commit startup handshake, then use owner EOF as the only retirement request.
- Remove finish, stop, retirement-marker, cleanup-acknowledgement, and directory-disposition messages and their owner-side state.
- Keep manager-failure monitoring as a process-only fallback and wait for successful manager exit as the primary cleanup barrier.
- Remove a regression that depended on the deleted stop-message failure path.

title: Emit managed plots when pages finalize
description:
## Summary

Managed R plots now enter the response when the PNG device actually finalizes each page. This follows the worker's natural sequence of events and removes the cell-wide output barrier and explicit cross-device ordering policy.

## User-facing changes

- A page finalized by opening another page is emitted at that point in the timeline, before later console output.
- Console text produced while a page remains open is emitted immediately and can precede the eventual image.
- Cell-end cleanup still closes managed devices and emits final pages, including after ordinary R errors and from Python's R bridge.
- Managed-device sizing, cell scope, and ownership are unchanged.

## Internal changes

- Publish a managed page directly after its original `newPage` or `close` callback returns.
- Remove the global page queue, deferred text chunks, and after-each-REPL-iteration drain.
- Keep the small C callback trampoline as the long-jump-safe boundary around R's device callbacks.
- Replace the exact cross-device-order transcript with a public page-finalization timeline regression.

title: Make MCP Console local-host-only
description:
Simplify MCP Console to local-host execution. Remove SSH, Docker, and Docker Sandbox support, including execution-target configuration and provider commands. For remote work, the documentation recommends running the MCP client and Console together on that host, alongside the client's shell and filesystem tools.

Internally, delete remote launch and retirement machinery, remote preparation protocols, prepared-runtime branches, and provider recording metadata. Move shared cancellable descriptor I/O into local process support, update tool descriptions, and remove provider documentation, examples, fixtures, and acceptance tests. Recordings and the private local preparation protocol are unversioned; the preparation client and child run from the same executable.

Windows companion snapshots still need regeneration on a native Windows host.

title: Delegate sandbox supervision to the private runner
description:
Make the sandbox command a thin application-policy frontend to the private runner. Console now execs the verified executable with immutable launch-time configuration, preserving the frontend PID, direct caller, standard streams, cancellation, and command status. The exact implementation pin is `b5a1c9f76a9c6ca2909105aecbc78555a26fda01`; protocol 2 and Rust 1.95.0 remain unchanged. Current main through `e37f8ab0` is merged, including the two-pipe worker sideband, automatic companion preparation for source installations, streaming bundle verification, release builds for integration tests, and Linux CPU-only PyTorch wheels. The original runner repository was not modified.

Console retains installation verification, ordinary server child-process integration, policy defaults, and every existing policy exception. Native supervision, terminal ownership, descendant retirement, and private storage belong to the runner.

```text
Before, macOS: caller/server → Console launcher → {Console manager, runner → target wrapper → target}
Before, Linux: caller/server → Console launcher → Console manager → runner/helpers → target wrapper → target
After:         caller/server → runner (original frontend PID) → native enforcement → target
```

The production diff deletes 16 files, removes 4,049 lines, and adds 228: a net deletion of 3,821 lines. This removes Console's manager, recovery monitor, descendant tracking, temporary-directory ownership, fork-and-continue path, setup writer, hidden target wrapper, and CLI variants. One retained startup-cancellation regression exposed a Console race that sent SIGKILL before runner retirement; the ordinary child join now requests SIGTERM and waits through the existing grace period before escalation.

Independent recovery after supervisor death is intentionally removed. Configured caller death still requires cleanup while the runner lives. Two CLI cases dedicated to supervisor-death cleanup are deleted. The Linux combined case keeps its original name and restores launcher-crash descendant termination; only that scenario's private-storage expectation changes. Command exit, owned SIGTERM, and caller-death records remain unchanged. Fixtures that detach children now wait for exact runner observation before orphaning them on macOS. Their original cleanup, status, output, and restart assertions remain. Five runner-native startup/prerequisite diagnostics have revised expectations. The retained supervisor-crash and stalled-supervisor MCP cases report explicit cleanup failures. Private temporary paths, directory-removal errors, storage retention after unproven retirement, and Linux mutation of the private data directory follow the runner's documented contract. Console adds no application-level request-size cap or new sandbox-policy exception. Fixed configuration shares the native exec byte budget; exact maximum-size parity was not tested.

The original macOS baseline passed 407 applicable transcript cases. The updated baseline at `26a5f3c3` passed 413, with all 431 snapshots unchanged; the later main poll-ownership case also passed against that saved executable. Both baselines passed core checks, all 47 Rust tests, and installed-runner acceptance. Local validation at the preceding PR head `5e4a5ccc` is recorded as follows:

| Scope                     | Result                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| macOS                     | `scripts/check` passed: core checks, 47 Rust tests, 409 public transcript cases; 10 unavailable cases.                                                                                              |
| Linux                     | Core checks and 47 Rust tests passed. Per-case inventory: 383 host cases passed, plus the procfs case in a container; 35 cases unavailable. Aggregate runs hit the two intermittent failures below. |
| Installed executable pair | macOS: five passed, two Linux-only skips. Linux: all seven passed in an Ubuntu container.                                                                                                           |
| Pinned runner contracts   | All 58 executable contracts passed on macOS; release runner builds passed on macOS and Linux.                                                                                                       |
| Snapshot comparison       | Only the four listed diagnostics change among retained records. Formatting-only regeneration was restored after parsed-equality checks.                                                             |

Linux host transcripts use the exact built bubblewrap under the host's existing AppArmor profile, via a test-only PATH wrapper. The nested-procfs prerequisite case runs separately in an Ubuntu container with namespace prerequisites enabled. The host's user R profile caused the first aggregate attempt to fail in an unsandboxed resolver case; the complete rerun disables that profile with `R_PROFILE_USER=/dev/null`, without changing the fixture or expectation. No host policy or sysctl was changed.

An aggregate Linux run also hit an unexplained SQL-interrupt timeout after 321 passing cases. The unchanged case passed a focused rerun and 12 repeated trials on this integration; it also passed 12 matched trials on main. Its assertion, 30-second deadline, and snapshot remain unchanged. A further aggregate run stopped after 175 passing cases because the R direct-stdin restart case missed its expected callback-release output; that case passed focused runs on both the integration and main. Both failures remain unexplained, although the subsequent hosted Ubuntu aggregate run passed. title: Transfer sandbox directory cleanup ownership to the manager
description:
## Summary

The sandbox manager already adopts the private temporary-directory guard before reporting readiness. This change makes that manager the only active guard after readiness, instead of keeping a duplicate guard in the owner-side monitor.

The owner retains its creation guard until readiness, then keeps only the canonical path needed to remove the directory after successful recovery before commitment begins. At `COMMIT`, it discards that path and leaves all later directory disposition to the manager. This removes the monitor's atomic preservation flags and makes the path lifetime represent the ownership state directly.

## User-facing behavior

There is no intended user-visible or private-protocol change. Startup gating, observed-descendant cleanup, committed manager-failure recovery, standalone exit status, terminal handling, cleanup deadlines, and final remove-or-preserve disposition remain unchanged.

## Internal changes

- disarm the owner guard only after manager readiness while keeping it armed through path canonicalization
- retain a raw recovery path before commitment and remove it only after successful pre-commit owner recovery
- restore fail-fast validation that the manager monitor exists before `COMMIT`
- remove the monitor-owned directory guard, preservation atomics and flags, and `mem::forget` preservation
- update the current ownership documentation

## Validation

- `scripts/test --jobs 1 cli/sandbox cli/sandbox_crash cli/sandbox_supervision client_server/sandbox_crash client_server/sandbox_startup`
- `scripts/check`

## Limitation

A Rust panic in the sandbox manager retains its existing behavior. This PR transfers the duplicate owner guard; it does not add a separate panic-recovery guarantee.

title: Make sandbox managers own sandbox lifetimes
description:
## Summary

Use one host-side sandbox manager as the primary lifetime owner for each macOS worker generation and standalone command. This removes split normal and crash cleanup ownership, so restart, replacement, shutdown, owner loss, and standalone retirement cross the same lifetime barrier.

## User-facing changes

- Keep the relay or standalone command behind a private startup gate until the manager has adopted the temporary directory, begun descendant observation, and confirmed ownership.
- Retire observed descendants after process-group or session changes while keeping the direct root waitable until cleanup completes.
- Preserve the private temporary directory whenever startup, ownership commitment, retirement, or manager recovery is ambiguous.
- Preserve standalone command exit status and startup errors when forwarded signals are already pending at a cleanup boundary, while retaining foreground-terminal behavior.

There is no MCP tool or relay-worker message-schema change.

## Internal changes

- Use a private Unix socket for readiness, ownership commitment, forced cleanup, and the standalone final directory disposition.
- Monitor manager exit from the host owner and perform bounded fallback cleanup from the still-pinned root when the manager fails.
- Keep whole-sandbox lifetime cleanup in the manager while the relay retains direct-worker supervision, local same-process-group cleanup, and transport responsibilities.
- Add public macOS transcript coverage for startup gates, ambiguous commitment, manager failure, bounded recovery, detached descendants, process-group rescan races, pending signals at root exit and commitment failure, and owner loss during retirement.

## Limitations

Darwin cannot atomically observe every fork. A descendant that becomes orphaned before manager observation, or that detached before fallback reconstruction, remains outside the cleanup guarantee. Linux and Windows remain unsupported.

## Additional notes

Local validation included `scripts/format`, `scripts/check`, repeated six-way `client_server/r` runs, an injected delayed-stdin relay probe, an injected manager EPERM and late-process-group-member rescan, repeated standalone crash regressions, and focused `cli/sandbox_supervision`, `client_server/sandbox_crash`, `client_server/sandbox_startup`, `client_server/sandbox_supervision`, and `client_server/zod` transcript suites.

title: Retire worker generations after abrupt server exit
description:
## Summary

Worker-generation cleanup previously depended on the server-owned observer. An uncatchable server exit could therefore leave an observed worker descendant running and its private temporary directory behind.

This change commits one independent macOS sandbox manager per worker generation. After readiness, the manager observes exact process identities, survives abrupt server loss, retires the descendants it observed, and attempts to remove the generation's private temporary directory.

## User-facing changes

- Abrupt `mcp-console serve` exit on macOS now retires descendants observed by the committed manager, including descendants that entered another process group or session.
- Normal restart, failure replacement, and orderly shutdown retain their existing server-owned behavior.
- The standalone `mcp-console sandbox` command is unchanged.

## Internal changes

- Add a hidden manager process with a fixed private initialization and retirement protocol on fd 0.
- Track the server, relay, and descendants by PID plus process start time. Crash cleanup never signals an unpinned raw process-group ID.
- Coordinate normal retirement through an explicit start, cleanup acknowledgement, direct-relay reap, and final remove-or-preserve disposition. A server exit during this handoff conservatively preserves the directory.
- Keep manager monitoring bounded before and after forced termination. If the manager is externally killed, the server observer and pinned process-group backstop complete generation retirement.
- Add public macOS regressions for server, relay, and manager failure, including a stopped-server race after relay exit. The tests use a detached standard-library Python child and causal FIFO/process-state checkpoints.
- Document the manager boundary, ownership order, failure behavior, and current limitations in the architecture and sandbox-supervision documentation.

## Limitations

Darwin cannot atomically attach the manager's observer during spawn. A descendant that becomes orphaned before the manager observes it remains outside crash cleanup even after readiness. Directory removal after server loss is best effort, and a server exit after normal retirement begins preserves the directory because the final success-or-error disposition is unknown. Linux and Windows remain unsupported.

## Testing

- `scripts/format`
- `scripts/check-core`
- `scripts/test --jobs 1`
- `scripts/test --jobs 6 client_server/zod::restart_drains_readable_frame_before_abandoning_partial_tail client_server/sandbox_crash`
- release wheel build and `scripts/release.py smoke-wheel`
- `R CMD build` and `R CMD check --no-manual` (`Status: OK`)

title: Reuse host caches in transcript tests
description:
## Summary

- let IR, uv, renv, pak, and DuckDB use their ambient resolver-owned cache locations in transcript tests
- remove temporary `HOME` isolation, cache-file assertions, and cache deletion from SQL and custom-worker tests
- explicitly prepare required Ragnar extensions and keep Zod assertions limited to worker-observable state

## Tests

- `./scripts/test -j 4`

title: Rename MCP tools to send and session
description:
## Summary

Rename the MCP-facing tool surface from `console` and `console_session` to `send` and `session`, and document `console` as the default client registration name.

Codex derives an MCP tool namespace from the client registration name. The previous names would therefore produce:

```text
mcp__mcp_console.console
mcp__mcp_console.console_session
```

The new convention produces the shorter:

```text
mcp__console.send
mcp__console.session
```

## Why these names

The frequent tool does more than evaluate code. It accepts a complete R, Python, or SQL cell, supplies `stdin` to an active evaluation, or waits and polls when called without either. Names such as `eval`, `run`, and `write` each describe only part of that interface. `submit` is closer but can imply a queued job. `send` is neutral across code and interactive input, and it matches the existing `mcp-console send` CLI command.

The lifecycle tool is named `session` because its `action` argument already identifies the operation, such as `prepare`, `interrupt`, `restart`, or `close`. Names such as `console_session` and `manage_session` would repeat information already supplied by the `console` namespace and the action.

`workbench` was also considered as the namespace, but it already has a distinct meaning in the surrounding project context.

## Constraints

- The package, executable, CLI, and MCP initialization identity remain `mcp-console`.
- The public MCP surface remains limited to two compact tools.
- Existing schemas and behavior do not change as part of the rename.
- The implemented `send` tool still echoes arbitrary JSON; `session` remains planned but unimplemented.
- The old tool names are removed rather than retained as compatibility aliases, since aliases would keep the redundant names in model context.
- Product-level console terminology, `.mcp-console` paths, service identifiers, synthetic source names, and CLI names remain unchanged.

## User-facing changes

- Rename the implemented `console` tool to `send`.
- Rename the planned `console_session` tool to `session`.
- Document `console` as the default client registration name.
- Update tool descriptions and examples to use the new names.

## Internal changes

- Rename the public transcript case and golden snapshot so `tools/list` and `tools/call` exercise `send`.
- Remove the old test helper alias.
- Update planned MCP module names and synchronize the design documents.

title: Prepare MCP Console 0.0.5 for PyPI
description:
Prepare the merged runtime and configuration features for the 0.0.5 PyPI release so users can install them without building Console from source.

The package version and generated CLI/MCP snapshots now identify 0.0.5. PyPI installation covers macOS and Linux on ARM64 and x86-64, plus a new experimental Windows x64 wheel. The guides describe Linux runtime libraries, the Windows Visual C++ runtime and sandbox setup, and source builds for development.

Windows builds use the PEP 517 backend so the public command retains its installed native bundle. Sandbox launches expand 8.3 working-directory aliases before the elevated helper checks profile access. The updated companion checks directory metadata access before sandbox logon, avoids unnecessary ACL writes when existing permissions suffice, and preserves child permissions when a grant is needed. Installed-wheel acceptance covers first startup from a short profile path, persistent state and restart, filesystem and exit-status enforcement, Python without R, and the R/Python bridge.

The release workflow requires five installed and smoke-tested artifacts and both native Linux floor checks, and pins uv to the same version as CI. Linux preparation uses the same Rscript path, R_HOME, and complete package request as runtime resolution, so startup can reuse its prepared cache. Runtime startup limits remain unchanged. Failures retain Windows stderr and sandbox logs, or Linux process ancestry, wait states, executable paths, selected preparation settings, and cached-library state. Checkpoint failures retain MCP and stderr context without changing their deadlines. Manual dispatch remains a build-only rehearsal.

After publishing, the workflow waits up to two minutes for all expected wheel filenames and SHA-256 digests in the version JSON and package index, including retries for temporary request failures. Visible hash mismatches, yanked files, and HTTP permission errors fail immediately. It then verifies fresh pinned and unqualified `uvx`/`uv tool install`, installed sandbox execution, and Python-only MCP on all five release platforms. Windows also exercises its R/Python bridge.

Windows acceptance checks native MXC capability through explicit public backend selection before provisioning legacy accounts. Capable hosts must execute the proxy workload successfully; unavailable hosts must reject explicit MXC and automatic proxy launches with the expected errors. Unexpected launch failures still fail acceptance. Resolver proxy acceptance uses a controlled local origin for the permitted host, preserving the policy and capture assertions without depending on an external TLS handshake. Publication timeout coverage gates a request after observing the incomplete package index, preserving the deadline and index assertions.

Local core and transcript checks, all four formatters, and 43 release-tool cases pass. Native Windows ACL and long-path checks pass. The physical Windows host has a separate runner-pipe startup failure, so full native application acceptance is required on the fresh hosted runner before publication.

title: Prepare version 0.0.4
description:
Bump the package to 0.0.4 for the next PyPI release. CLI output, MCP discovery, and target compatibility diagnostics now report the new version.

Synchronize Cargo metadata and regenerate the matching public transcript snapshots.

Keep release builds on native runners with `container: off`. The previous `manylinux: off` setting forced Linux wheel tags that PyPI rejects; leaving tag selection to Maturin allows the four-platform release to publish.

title: Prepare release 0.0.3
description:
Prepare 0.0.3 as the last release with the in-project sandbox implementation.

Bump the package version in Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock, regenerate CLI and MCP version snapshots, and update the release guide and its requirement for successful CI on the exact release commit. Runtime behavior is unchanged apart from the reported version.

title: Make worker retirement an ordered lifecycle boundary
description:
## Summary

Worker failure and replacement previously shared a delayed restart notice without sharing a clear lifecycle boundary. Output accepted from the old worker could therefore be reported after replacement output.

This change defines one causal sequence: close worker input and request protocol shutdown, stop and reap the process by the existing deadline, finish the active sideband operation, cancel and join the standard-stream readers, join the stdin task, and only then report that the worker stopped or launch its replacement. Sideband content, standard-stream bytes, failures, and lifecycle facts now use one typed pending output tape.

## User-facing changes

- Infrastructure and protocol failures return retained worker output, the specific bracketed error, and `[worker stopped: in-memory state lost]` in that order.
- Every replacement attempt emits `[starting new worker]` before launch, so startup output and startup errors follow that notice. Initial lazy startup remains silent.
- Explicit restart returns old-worker output, including sideband images, before the stopped notice, starting notice, replacement startup output, and `[restarted]`.
- A `[running]`, `[stdin needed]`, or `[idle]` response drains output produced so far before appending its state banner.
- When restart cancels a waiting `send`, that call receives a concise cancellation error and restart remains the next output boundary.
- Requirement preparation racing active worker startup reports `worker is busy`; another concurrent preparation continues to report `session is preparing requirements`.

## Why this was restarted

The first attempt in #59 treated this as a banner-ordering bug. It reserved a pending restart notice before replacement startup and committed the notice after the replacement reported ready.

That patch grew during review because each timing case added another conditional notice, output handoff, or lifecycle flag. The repeated findings pointed to the underlying problem: the code was repairing output order after the fact without defining the point where the old worker could no longer publish output.

PR #59 was closed, and this implementation was rebuilt from a fresh `origin/main`. The final design centers the existing shutdown path and physical I/O cutoff, then records lifecycle facts in the same output sequence as worker output. The last cleanup replaced the separate evaluation and standard-stream buffers with one typed tape and removed the restart-output transfer state.

## Internal changes

- `Running(Worker)` is the finalization owner. It retains the sideband reader and the tasks for stdin, stdout, and stderr. Lifecycle state keeps a cloneable shutdown capability that closes stdin, sends the protocol shutdown message, waits until the deadline, and force-stops the process group if needed. This path does not send `SIGINT`.
- Retirement completes only after the active sideband operation releases the worker, the owner cancels and joins its standard-stream readers, and its stdin task ends. The stopped notice is appended after that boundary, and replacement launch begins afterward.
- Each standard-stream reader polls its worker pipe and a generation-owned cancellation pipe. Retirement closes the cancellation pipe after the direct worker stops, so a background descendant retaining fd 1 or 2 cannot keep restart or shutdown open.
- One typed output tape stores raw standard-stream chunks, sideband text and images, failures, and lifecycle notices. Restart changes which response may drain the tape; it does not move output between buffers.
- Physical worker state remains `Initial`, `Stopped`, or `Running`. Evaluation/input timing and session restart/shutdown remain separate concerns rather than compound worker states.
- Send and requirement preparation use a read/write admission boundary, keeping preparation cancellation independent from evaluation response ownership.
- Startup failure, automatic failure, explicit restart, and server shutdown use the same retirement boundary. Public transcript coverage and protocol documentation describe the resulting order.

## Notes

Background descendants that escape the supported worker process-group lifetime remain unsupervised and may outlive the worker. Retirement closes their inherited standard-stream capture, so they cannot extend the old worker's output boundary or publish after its stopped notice.

title: Refactor worker launch through runtime boundary
description:
## Summary
