Introduce a small private worker-runtime boundary that separates launch inputs, worker spawning, and lifecycle control. This gives future sandbox and runtime work a clearer extension point without selecting a provider or changing the current execution model.

## User-facing changes

None. Worker startup, protocol behavior, sandbox policy, restart and shutdown semantics, and platform support remain unchanged.

## Internal changes

- Collect the inputs for one current-runtime launch in `WorkerSpec`.
- Route macOS and unsupported-platform worker startup through `WorkerRuntime::spawn()`.
- Rename the internal `StopHandle` to `WorkerHandle` to describe its lifecycle role.
- Update the implemented worker-protocol and repository documentation.

title: Simplify Python Responses adapters and cancel interrupted waits
description:
`MCPConsole` now forwards a host `KeyboardInterrupt` to the SDK's request cancellation and re-raises it. An admitted cell keeps running, so callers can catch Ctrl-C and poll for output or send `control="interrupt"` explicitly.

The synchronous client keeps its AnyIO bridge to the official MCP Python SDK, which owns transport and protocol handling. Responses adapters now share schema, argument, and result conversion helpers and call their respective clients directly, removing the sync adapter's dependency on the async adapter and the client's generic execution helper. The `send()` arguments, live tool schemas, and text/image outputs are preserved.

The Python guide documents the background event loop, host cancellation, and sending control calls from another thread.

title: Separate worker lifecycle from R integration
description:
## Summary

The worker coordinator now uses a small optional R integration for event-aware waiting, idle callbacks, graphics, and interrupt checks. Shared command readiness, cell bookkeeping, input finalization, shutdown observation, and completion publication can run without initializing R. This removes the lifecycle dependency on an R instance while keeping one coordinator and one cell-dispatch path.

Ordinary sessions still initialize R eagerly. Its event-aware wait, pending and suspended interrupt state, Python-preparation deferral, and graphics hooks around R and Python cells remain in place. The internal native path uses the existing sideband and interrupt wakeups, observes stdin closure, and acknowledges each interrupt once. Public behavior and protocols are unchanged.

Subprocess coverage exercises native waiting, interrupt acknowledgment, and shutdown without R. The selected mixed-language, input, interrupt, idle-callback, graphics, and lifecycle transcripts passed before and after the change. Local `scripts/check` passed on `c979c5dd` (core checks, full transcripts, and source and wheel installation). The production diff is **367 additions plus deletions**.

title: Share typed events between the journal and recording projections
description:
The recorder and its Markdown and Quarto projections now share typed events. This removes field-by-field validation of internally constructed JSON, the duplicate schema-version constant, and checks for impossible projection states.

The journal schema and payloads, raw rejected requests, image artifacts, and generated Markdown and Quarto contents are preserved. Serialization happens at the journal boundary; projections render the same event directly in memory. This is an internal refactor with no change to the console interface.

title: Separate the SQL runtime facade from its DBI backend
description:
## Summary

Establish a worker-facing SQL runtime facade around the current embedded-R DuckDB/DBI implementation.

- keep worker dispatch dependent only on `src/sql.rs`
- move ownership of the R bridge source and DBI-backed runtime into `src/sql/dbi.rs`
- preserve the existing persistent catalog, R/Python interoperability, Arrow query path, preview rendering, interrupts, and output behavior

This is the SQL counterpart to the Python backend boundary introduced in #149. It creates the seam needed to change or replace the SQL host later without coupling that work to worker dispatch.

## Scope

This is an internal source-boundary refactor. It does not move SQL into Python, add a Python-only or no-R worker, change the worker or relay protocols, alter dependency resolution, or intentionally change any transcript.

## Validation

The branch is based directly on current `main` after #162. The change is awaiting the repository's macOS GitHub Actions checks; no golden transcripts were edited.

title: Use a Unix socket for the worker sideband
description:
## Summary

Represent the worker sideband as the full-duplex connection it already is. This replaces two inherited anonymous pipes with one unnamed Unix stream socket pair while preserving JSONL framing, message schemas, lifecycle behavior, and per-direction ordering.

## User-facing changes

Custom workers now receive one inherited `MCP_CONSOLE_SIDEBAND_FD` endpoint instead of separate read and write descriptors. The implemented worker protocol documentation describes the new launch contract.

## Internal changes

The relay and worker share each endpoint through `Arc<UnixStream>`, with a reader-local framing buffer and a writer-only serialization lock. Normal reads and writes remain blocking. Retirement uses per-call `MSG_DONTWAIT` receives so cancellation can forward complete immediately readable frames without changing the socket's shared blocking mode.

The built-in worker, deterministic custom worker, and worker-sideband proxy now use one endpoint. The proxy preserves directional closure with local write-side shutdowns, and fork children close their inherited descriptor without shutting down the parent's endpoint.

title: Refactor worker command dispatch
description:
## Summary

Move the built-in worker's process-lifetime bridges and sideband writer into a `Runtime`, and separate the receive loop from per-command dispatch. This gives later worker-loop changes one command handler without duplicating evaluation, preparation, or shutdown behavior.

## User-facing changes

None. The worker accepts the same messages and returns the same results.

## Internal changes

`Runtime::run()` owns command receipt, while `Runtime::handle()` owns evaluation, requirement preparation, resolver-response validation, and shutdown dispatch. Returning a boolean from `handle()` keeps shutdown explicit without changing the protocol.

title: Make Python runtime setup independent of reticulate
description:
## Summary

Console now installs its native Python services, private evaluator, SQL adapter, and automatic-import configuration through one post-initialization setup path. This removes the reticulate adapter and its Python string dispatcher from the setup dependency, so a caller with a known interpreter can complete setup without loading R.

Ordinary sessions still initialize R eagerly. Reticulate still selects the interpreter, attaches conversion and event integration, supplies the converted resolver callback, and installs its R-specific hooks. Native setup runs after reticulate's competing stream and input hooks. Requirement preparation, resolver behavior, module-load timing, and public protocols remain unchanged.

The retained CPython state records completed setup steps and marks configuration complete only after the native call succeeds. A subprocess regression initializes a fixture-specified interpreter without libR, evaluates successive cells in the ordinary embedded evaluator, and checks state, output, error recovery, disabled automatic resolution, and repeated setup.

Validation: `scripts/check` passed on `e8a26aba`, including core checks, the full transcript suite, and installation checks. The focused startup and automatic-resolution suites also passed. The production diff is 318 additions plus 120 deletions, 438 lines total, measured with `scripts/review-diff origin/main`.

title: Separate shared worker services from embedded R
description:
Separate shared worker coordination from embedded R as the first step toward an R-optional worker. This is an internal, behavior-preserving refactor: the worker still eagerly initializes R and uses the existing R, Python, and SQL evaluators. Running without R is not supported by this change.

The runtime-neutral services now own command readiness, active cell-language bookkeeping and the SQL resolution gate, native SIGINT distribution, managed-input wakeup setup, and Python interrupt acknowledgment. The R adapter supplies state-only callbacks for interrupt recording, acceptance, and clearing so nested R/Python calls still share R's pending and suspended state. Shared services neither access R globals directly nor enter R.

The coordinator keeps R's event-aware wait and idle servicing and separates cell bookkeeping from graphics hooks. Both R and Python cells still run R graphics hooks, including when Python calls R; SQL retains its existing exclusion. Evaluation, error, input cleanup, and completion ordering are preserved. Startup passes the existing R session temporary directory to Python cache setup with the same location and cleanup ownership.

R startup, REPL input routing, interrupt checks and deferral, native error/unwind boundaries, event processing, and graphics remain in the R adapter. Reticulate startup and attachment, interpreter selection, requirement storage and activation, SQL providers, and initialization policy remain unchanged. The release and installation fixtures now mirror native source paths, including the extracted signal glue. There are no public API or transcript expectation changes.

The focused compatibility transcripts and full `scripts/check` pass on macOS, including source and wheel installations, with unchanged transcript expectations. Existing capability-dependent skips remain.

title: Simplify sandbox policy capture and forwarding
description:
Sandbox launches rebuilt application policy from separate settings, and the server and frontend each implemented environment precedence. Capture Console's application additions once and share the environment handling to reduce that duplication.

Internally, the settings handoff now carries native policy JSON directly. Writable roots, the runtime marker, and platform additions are incorporated during capture; each launch adds its protocol and lifetime requirements. Tool descriptions read the captured values without repeating defaults. Native validation and defaults remain the runner's responsibility.

This is an internal refactor with no user-facing behavior changes. The diff reduces production code by 56 lines across five files and changes no tests or snapshots. Verified with the existing public sandbox regressions, full macOS `scripts/check`, and focused Linux checks.

Follow-up to #296.

title: Share readiness waits between sideband and worker relay
description:
Sideband I/O and the worker relay duplicated the same blocking readiness loop. Move descriptor setup, interrupted-wait retries, and readiness reporting into `src/readiness.rs` so they have one implementation.

This is an internal refactor with no user-facing changes. Callers retain their cancellation behavior, including the sideband writer's existing error and the relay's buffered-output draining.

Local validation passed on macOS: core checks, all 47 Rust tests, all 463 applicable transcript cases with `scripts/test --jobs 4`, and source/wheel installation checks. At default concurrency, `scripts/check` stopped on a worker-readiness timeout in `cli/relay/test_worker_pipe`; the same timeout reproduced on unchanged `main`.

title: Use anonymous pipes for the worker sideband
description:
Replace the relay-worker sideband socket pair with two anonymous pipes, one for each direction. Public MCP behavior remains unchanged. The private custom-worker bootstrap now supplies `MCP_CONSOLE_SIDEBAND_READ_FD` and `MCP_CONSOLE_SIDEBAND_WRITE_FD`; workers adopt both descriptors, remove both variables, and isolate the endpoints from fork and exec descendants.

Internally, nonblocking I/O and readiness polling preserve ordered JSONL messages and backpressure. Separate cancellation wakeups bound relay reader and writer joins, including when a pipe is full or a descendant retains its endpoints. Retirement keeps the existing deadline, drains complete buffered or readable frames, and abandons incomplete tails. Pipe writes report EPIPE without invoking or replacing the runtime's SIGPIPE handler.

Executable regressions cover the bootstrap, bidirectional exchange, partial and interrupted I/O, blocked-writer cancellation, partial frames, peer death, retained endpoints, and fork/exec isolation. Existing transport fixtures now use pipes; existing observable snapshots and deadlines are preserved.

Sandbox policies, enforcement, launch behavior, supervision, cleanup, process topology, signal restoration, and the sandbox runner's source pin, installation, and invocation are unchanged.

`scripts/check` passed on macOS. On Linux, `scripts/check-core` and all 27 selected transcript cases passed, covering the pipe regressions, shutdown, transport, streams, and fork/exec isolation. Full local Linux validation previously hit the host UID-map restriction, a Quarto preparation failure also reproduced on pre-refactor main, and parallel startup checkpoint failures; isolated and serial targeted runs pass. Hosted checks are pending on the latest commit.

title: Share macOS sandbox kqueue primitives
description:
## Summary

Descendant tracking and standalone root observation previously owned separate `kqueue` implementations with duplicated descriptor, registration, wakeup, timeout, and error handling. This refactor moves those Darwin primitives into one internal wrapper while leaving lifecycle policy and event interpretation at their existing call sites.

## User-facing changes

- None. Sandbox behavior, diagnostics, protocols, and platform support remain unchanged.

## Internal changes

- Add one `Kqueue` owner for process, user, and signal registrations, wakeups, waits, and timeout conversion.
- Preserve a strong queue handle for standalone manager wakeups and a weak handle for process-tracker stop requests, including descriptor pinning during each trigger.
- Centralize `EINTR` retries and process-watch `ESRCH` classification. Process watch registration and best-effort deletion now use the same `EINTR` retry rule as the other queue submissions.
- Keep event batching, ordering, and root-versus-wakeup precedence in the existing tracker and root-waiter paths. The refactor removes 68 net lines of production code.

## Validation

- `scripts/test cli/sandbox_supervision`
- `scripts/test cli/sandbox_crash`
- `scripts/test client_server/sandbox_supervision`
- `scripts/test client_server/sandbox_crash`
- `scripts/test client_server/sandbox_startup`
- `scripts/check`
- [GitHub Actions macOS CI](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/actions/runs/33666057512/job/100367973335)

title: Resolve managed Python versions directly in Rust
description:
## Summary

Move managed Python interpreter inventory and version selection from a helper R process into server-owned Rust. This removes an R and jsonlite subprocess from the worker callback path while keeping managed environment creation and Python evaluation on reticulate.

## User-facing changes

- Preserve reticulate's default ranking, abbreviated numeric constraints, and managed or system source preference.
- Match normalized PEP 440 version spellings and preserve prerelease ordering.
- Fall back to the system inventory when the managed inventory contains no supported default CPython interpreter.
- Report the direct `uv` exit status and stderr without synthetic R or jsonlite diagnostics.

## Internal changes

- Run `uv python list` directly with closed stdin and the existing generation-scoped cancellation path.
- Query managed and system inventories separately, tag their source explicitly, merge them, and rank them once against a global preferred-minor baseline.
- Resolve `RETICULATE_UV=managed` through reticulate and use the same executable, cache directory, and Python installation directory for direct inventory and environment creation.
- Remove the unused `python_version.R` program and update the runtime-source inventory, repository map, requirements documentation, fixtures, and public transcript coverage.

## Limitations

Managed environment creation, Python evaluation, and object conversion remain on reticulate. Direct version discovery uses interpreters that `uv` can find under the server's startup `PATH`; it does not add reticulate's separately registered virtualenv directories.

## Validation

- `scripts/format`
- `scripts/test client_server/python`
- `cargo test --test cli stdio_console_uses_reticulate_managed_uv_for_python_versions -- --nocapture`
- `scripts/check`

title: Remove the R Arrow dependency from SQL previews
description:
Console no longer requires or automatically prepares the R `arrow` package for SQL previews. Remove it from the default and runtime requirements, dependency warmups, and package documentation.

Internally, export the existing bounded Nanoarrow batch directly through DuckDB's registration callbacks for SQL casts. This preserves exact BIGINT, DECIMAL, and nested values, the preview limits, and single execution of the submitted SQL. The public regression now runs with an R library that excludes Arrow and checks that its namespace stays unloaded.

title: Remove redundant platform conditionals
description:
Remove redundant per-item platform guards as preparation for Linux support, reducing conditional-compilation noise in #251.

Keep platform selection at runtime and module boundaries, including one guard for the Python runtime, and retain the unsupported-platform stubs. The cleanup is internal; macOS behavior and existing tests and snapshots are unchanged.

title: Initialize CPython through the Rust runtime facade
description:
## Summary

Move CPython interpreter initialization behind the Rust runtime facade while keeping reticulate as the conversion and evaluation backend. Rust now owns the selected process-lifetime libpython handle, interpreter configuration, initialization, and initial GIL release.

This separates interpreter ownership from the current backend without changing the public console protocol or Python and SQL evaluation model.

## User-facing behavior

Python evaluation, managed requirements, plots, interrupts, debugger input, and console input retain their existing behavior. Python input continues to emit managed input-request records instead of reading deferred input directly from file descriptor 0.

Background Python threads remain runnable after initialization, including when a later reticulate initialization hook fails.

## Internal changes

- Retain the CPython program-name and Python-home buffers for the interpreter lifetime and mirror CPython's SIGPIPE setup through `PyOS_setsig`.
- Release the initial GIL when reticulate's C initializer returns or unwinds.
- Install the managed input bridge before reticulate's mutable initialization hooks.
- Preserve the external-attach path when Python was initialized before the initializer is installed.
- Remove the older stacked libpython-loading wrapper and update the implemented architecture and source map.

Reticulate still owns R and Python conversion, evaluation, managed requirements, event handling, and interrupts. This does not add a sans-R worker mode, and SQL behavior is unchanged.

## Testing

- `scripts/check`
- Release wheel build and installed-wheel smoke test with maturin 1.14.1
- Focused initialization, retry, input, debugger, automatic requirement, relay-output, and fork-output transcripts
- Python input and failed-initialization-hook coverage across CPython 3.10.20, 3.11.15, 3.12.14, 3.13.15, and 3.14.7

title: Load libpython through the Rust runtime facade
description:
## Summary

Build on #149 by moving process-lifetime ownership of the selected Python shared library into the Rust-owned runtime facade, while retaining reticulate as the current initialization, conversion, and evaluation backend.

## Changes

- Wrap reticulate's internal `py_initialize` entry point and pass the exact selected `libpython` path to Rust immediately before interpreter initialization.
- Load that library with eager global symbol visibility, verify the CPython API is present, and retain the handle for the worker process lifetime.
- Reject attempts to switch to a different shared library after one has been loaded.
- Attach the Rust-owned handle when startup code initialized reticulate before the MCP Console Python bridge was installed.

The worker and relay protocols are unchanged, and this is intended to preserve all existing transcripts.

## Scope

This PR does not yet call `Py_Initialize` directly, add a no-R worker mode, change runtime threading, or move SQL out of the current R/DBI backend. It establishes the dynamic-library ownership boundary needed for the next direct-CPython slice.

## Validation

- [ ] `scripts/check` through the macOS GitHub Actions workflow

title: Separate the Python runtime facade from its reticulate backend
description:
## Summary

Establish an internal Rust-owned Python runtime facade around the current reticulate backend.

- make `python.rs` the worker-facing runtime facade
- move the current R/reticulate bridge implementation, backend-specific environment configuration, embedded source ownership, and registered R callbacks into `python/reticulate.rs`
- preserve Python evaluation, preparation, managed resolution, plotting, interrupts, and transcript behavior

## Scope

This is an internal source-boundary refactor. It does not change the MCP protocol or user-facing built-in runtime behavior.

This PR does not initialize CPython directly, add a no-R mode, change runtime threading, or move SQL out of the current DBI/DuckDB implementation. It isolates the existing reticulate backend so later changes do not need to alter worker dispatch or the public protocol.

## Testing

- `scripts/format`
- `scripts/check`, including runtime-source validation, release tests, Rust formatting, Clippy with warnings denied, Rust tests, and the full transcript suite with no golden changes
- Python package build and smoke test
- R package build and `R CMD check`

title: Extract runtime programs and simplify repository guidance
description:
## Summary

Production R and Python programs now live in module-owned `.R` and `.py` files instead of Rust raw strings. Rust embeds them at compile time, so the binary remains self-contained while editors, formatters, and syntax checks can work with each language directly.

`AGENTS.md` now contains repository-wide ownership rules, development commands, and a source map instead of duplicating the detailed runtime specification.

## User-facing changes

- MCP tools and the worker and relay protocols are unchanged.
- R, Python, SQL, graphics, resolver, restart, and replacement behavior is unchanged.
- Existing transcript goldens are unchanged.

## Internal changes

- Extracted the Python, SQL, managed-graphics, and live R-library bridges, the private Python runtime, and four host resolver programs into source files under their owning modules.
- Supplied the Python runtime to its R bridge once through a private Rust callback that returns the compile-time source before reticulate can initialize Python.
- Added a check that inventories every extracted source, matches it to a Rust `include_str!`, rejects unresolved placeholders, parses R without evaluation, and validates Python 3.10 syntax without imports or bytecode.
- Updated the worker protocol source map and reduced `AGENTS.md` from 60 KB to a concise repository guide.

title: Remove provisional Python preparation state
description:
## Summary

Remove the transitional provisional-Python lifecycle state now that activation and explicit preparation receipts update the single retained managed-Python environment directly. This keeps the simplified receipt model from retaining a second copy solely for restart-required handling.

## User-facing changes

A successful explicit Python preparation retains the environment it actually activated even when an earlier background resolution produced an unactivated candidate. Other managed Python activation, failure, and restart behavior is unchanged.

## Internal changes

Consume resolved candidates when their activation receipts are accepted and discard all earlier candidates, so payload-free `python_prepared` cannot overwrite the accepted environment. Retain an unconsumed materialization candidate at `python_prepared`, remove the duplicate end-of-preparation commit, and delete the provisional environment copy from requirement-change state and resolver fallback.

title: Separate Python bootstrap from reticulate attachment
description:
Separate CPython bootstrap from the optional reticulate adapter so R-specific selection and attachment state stays with the bridge. The Python facade now retains that adapter directly, removing the intermediate `startup::Runtime` wrapper. Native bootstrap remains in `startup.rs`, and the retained CPython library continues to own interpreter lifetime and shared setup completion.

There are no intended user-facing changes. Interpreter selection, lazy Python initialization in R sessions, setup retries, managed requirements, SQL, and worker lifecycle behavior retain their existing paths and ordering.

Add a public MCP test that runs the same Python cells with R absent, with an R cell first, and with a Python cell first. It compares complete output and tracebacks, checks interpreter identity and persistent state, and adds bridge checks only when R is present. The same test runs directly and under the native sandbox. Update the architecture documentation and repository map to describe the ownership boundary.

This is a limited step toward independent runtime composition. R still initializes eagerly when available; reticulate-mediated selection and environment setup remain. Unifying those paths and supporting late runtime attachment require further work.

title: Call Python runtime setup through native CPython
description:
Route `activate_process_environment(executable)` and `disable_matplotlib_show` through Console's retained CPython library, continuing the work toward making R optional. This removes their reticulate-mediated `dispatch_python()` calls while keeping the helper implementations in Python. There are no public API or behavior changes.

Reticulate still activates the environment first; Console completes process-environment setup before recording pending activation. The early initialization branch still only updates `sys.executable`. Matplotlib setup retains its module-load hook and first-cell lifecycle points. The native entry points protect R conversions while preserving the caller's interrupt state during Python execution. Setup exceptions retain their original traceback and pass through reticulate's existing R condition and interrupt conversion without native printing.

R remains required and eagerly initialized. Reticulate still selects the interpreter, orchestrates startup, calculates requirement transitions, checks compatibility, and activates environments. The automatic-import resolver callback and its registration remain in the R adapter, including their dispatcher use.

Public acceptance coverage checks R-first initialization, child interpreter selection after late activation, Matplotlib calls from both languages, retry after interrupted setup, and a setup error reported once. Running-cell interruption uses the existing FIFO fixture; setup interruption synchronizes on a visible input request before sending a real interrupt. The error case checks both complete diagnostic streams before canonicalizing their arrival order.

`scripts/check` passed on macOS at `b4cc6d5d`, including core checks, all applicable public transcripts in direct and sandboxed modes, and source/wheel installation checks.

title: Move managed Python activation bookkeeping into Rust
description:
Move managed Python activation bookkeeping from the R bridge into Console's native requirement store, continuing the behavior-preserving work toward Console-owned environment management. There are no public API changes or changes to existing transcript expectations.

Rust now owns the pending activation key, checks the subsequent requirement write for a match, commits the copied requirement object, clears the pending state, and publishes `PythonActivated`. The adapter records the key only after reticulate activation and process-environment setup succeed. Requirement writes without a pending activation do not notify, including lazy declarations, no-op updates, and failed-preparation snapshot restoration. Pre-initialization preparation still materializes requirements without activating Python. The initial successful reticulate initialization hook publishes through the same native owner at its existing, separate lifecycle point.

The requirement store remains R-dependent. It preserves one authoritative R object, including field presence, vector attributes, history, and copy isolation; the pending key exists only until the matching commit. R-object protection stays on the existing thread, and native borrows end before R allocation, comparison, protection release, or notification publication. Reticulate still calculates requirement transitions, discovers and selects the interpreter, orchestrates startup, checks compatibility, and activates environments. The bridge retains normalization, process-environment setup, and preparation callbacks. This does not change initialization timing or add rollback guarantees for interpreter or environment mutations.

The focused Python requirement and lifecycle transcripts and full `scripts/check` pass on macOS, including source and wheel installation checks, with existing capability-dependent skips.

title: Store the worker Python manifest behind native accessors
description:
Store the managed worker's current Python requirement object in a passive native module, accessed through the existing R active binding. This is a small foundation extracted from #350 so later environment ownership changes can be reviewed separately.

The native store holds one GC-protected R value and returns copies, preserving field presence, ordering, vector attributes, class, and history without normalization. The R closure no longer retains a separate current manifest. Reticulate still owns requirement transitions, interpreter startup, compatibility checks, activation, and the automatic-import callback route. The server retains requirements at the same materialization and activation boundaries. R remains eager and managed SQL remains R-backed.

Two public cases cover requirement values and metadata, unchanged error behavior, and explicit materialization of lazy declarations without initializing Python. Existing startup, restart, failure, and retention cases remain unchanged. The only new snapshots record those two cases; there are no intended public behavior changes.

The existing requirements suite passed before implementation, and 61 related cases passed after it. `scripts/preflight`, all four formatters, and `git diff --check` passed. Full `scripts/check` passed on clean head `278d8c446dfbbdf815ce8917a6198ec58db61a2a` on macOS ARM64, including Clippy, Rust tests, the complete applicable transcript suite, and source/wheel installation checks. There were 54 platform/capability skips, including Linux-specific, Docker, Docker Sandbox, external SSH, and host-specific negative/crash cases. Linux was not validated locally.

Native environment transitions and activation, including the deferred review findings in #350, are outside this extraction. The fixture fixes from #351 landed separately on main and are outside this PR diff.

title: Accept managed Python activation receipts
description:
## Summary

Add a reserved `python_activated` worker receipt so the server can retain a managed Python environment when an evaluation or explicit preparation reports a successful activation. This establishes the server-side acceptance boundary before the built-in worker begins emitting the receipt.

## User-facing changes

There is no supported user-facing behavior change. The built-in worker continues to use terminal Python checkpoints in this layer.

## Internal changes

- Match activation receipts against environments resolved during the active operation or the already-retained environment.
- Retain a matching environment immediately while preserving terminal checkpoint validation.
- Reject managed Python activation receipts from custom workers with a specific protocol error.
- Document the new frame and state transition, with fixture coverage for custom-worker rejection.

## Notes

Replace the inherited direct-fd-0 restart regression's timer with explicit gate and checkpoint synchronization. This is test-only and does not change runtime behavior.

title: Simplify Python bridge initialization
description:
## Summary

Initialize `PYTHON_BRIDGE_INIT` by evaluating the R-level `eval(str2expression(source))` call. The bridge is fixed R source, so this keeps its parsing in R and removes the Rust-side parse-status and expression-count handling.

## User-facing changes

None. Python cell behavior and error handling remain unchanged.

## Internal changes

- Build the nested R call and evaluate it through the existing `R_tryEval` boundary.
- Preserve the returned private environment as before.
- Remove the manual `R_ParseVector`, parse-status, and expression-count plumbing.

title: Separate production owners and share startup and relay logic
description:
Separate production source by responsibility and remove repeated orchestration paths so configuration preparation, sends, inline control, ordered event dispatch, and relay I/O are easier to find and maintain.

There are no intentional user-facing changes. MCP schemas and tool prose, requirement semantics, output and recording, wire formats, target policies, and eager startup retain their existing contracts.

Internally, the worker client has focused configuration, send, control, and execution modules, with operation state separate from ordered dispatch. MCP arguments and captured tool presentation have separate owners. The relay has focused supervisor, command, stream, and descriptor modules; its existing event writer stays intact.

Startup builds an owned configuration and transcript for the original pending client instead of constructing and discarding another client. Ordinary launches share their failure cleanup, timed startup waits consume readiness once, and worker-directed relay commands share one sideband forwarding path. The two incremental JSONL readers share framing that scans new bytes, decodes completed slices, and compacts after a drained batch while retaining their own I/O and retirement policies. The empty child-exit forwarding module is removed.

The PR updates navigation, adds focused framing tests, and supplies the selected R launcher's shell prerequisite in the isolated discovery fixture. That fixture correction addresses failures observed on clean main before the refactor; assertions and snapshots are unchanged.

title: Share Python import control and runtime setup
description:
Managed Python imports and Python-only setup use different paths depending on whether R is available. Share their runtime machinery so both compositions follow the same reached-import resolution and setup behavior, while the server continues to own accepted environments and worker generations.

User-visible changes:

- Reject incompatible inspected candidates before interpreter mutation. Unsafe R activation failures retain the worker and require restart before further requirement changes, including failures during preparation or idle callbacks.
- Apply NumPy, pandas, and Matplotlib defaults through common Python setup. Preserve nondefault startup widths and later user overrides.
- Allow interrupted common setup, including managed import configuration, to retry without replacing the interpreter or its Python objects.
- Initialize shared managed state when an R startup package has already started Python. Preserve existing objects and the running environment through attachment, and enable reached-import resolution.

Internally, the shared requirement owner replaces the separate native worker state, reticulate candidate slot, and R import-resolution callback. The R compatibility adapter retains declaration metadata, conditions, history, and protected object lifetimes. Activation uses the execution host's inspected identity; reticulate obtains additional conversion metadata from that exact executable without generic interpreter rediscovery. Initial activation publication follows worker readiness, and setup completion includes the import policy.

Private launch and SSH compatibility advance to version 6 because Python activation-failure receipts are now valid during preparation and idle callbacks. Preparation remains version 5; the public tool surface is unchanged.

Shared public cases cover resolver failure, cancellation, candidate rejection, unsafe activation, startup adoption, and setup retry. Additional coverage verifies that idle `later` callbacks run and deliver output through the next Python or SQL response without another R cell.

This is an intermediate peer-runtime increment. R still initializes eagerly, ordinary Python startup with R still requires reticulate attachment, and idle tool preparation still has separate R-backed and R-free orchestration. An external startup package can select its original environment again on restart; accepted declarations survive, but adoption does not replay activation into that already-running interpreter. Process prerequisites, actual late R attachment, and the prepared-target R-only gap remain documented in `design-sketches/peer-runtime-completion.md`.

title: Share Python bootstrap across runtime compositions
description:
Python previously received different environment setup depending on whether R was available, and mixed-runtime launches discarded part of the inspected Python identity. This change gives both compositions one Console-owned bootstrap and retains independent R and Python selections through local, SSH, Docker, and Docker Sandbox launches.

Explicit virtualenvs preserve their executable spelling, prefixes, and subprocess interpreter. Console applies PATH, VIRTUAL_ENV, and the effective PYTHONPATH before startup hooks; reticulate attaches without replaying activation scripts or rewriting the interpreter environment. RETICULATE_PYTHONPATH now supplies the interpreter and child-process environment consistently. Ordinary R evaluation still leaves Python uninitialized. When an R startup package has already initialized Python, Console attaches to its existing identity and preserves its objects and environment.

Internally, this removes the exclusive R-or-Python launch enum, the lossy inspection projection, the separate R environment initializer, and the path-only R resolver response. Managed candidates carry execution-host inspection through the existing activation and acceptance transactions, so restart retains the accepted identity. Private launch and preparation protocols advance to version 5. The shared peer-runtime tests cover standalone execution, virtualenv hooks and children, actual Python initialization state, managed activation and replacement, and remote resolver ownership.

This is a substantive bootstrap increment toward peer runtimes. R remains eager, and managed declaration adaptation still has R-specific and R-free paths. The architecture documentation describes that boundary; `design-sketches/peer-runtime-completion.md` specifies the remaining declaration-owner work and the loader, interrupt, storage, callback, and SQL prerequisites for late R initialization, with acceptance tests. No runtime threads or public runtime-selection interface are added.

title: Extract native managed Python activation boundary
description:
Live managed Python activation now has an R-free native entry point. This removes reticulate values and callbacks from the activation-time compatibility decision and failure result, so an already-running native CPython caller can activate a resolved candidate.

The operation takes the candidate's selected Python path, `libpython`, and executable, plus the running interpreter's `libpython`. It compares the library identities exactly before changing the live interpreter and distinguishes incompatibility, infrastructure failure, and an exception retained with its original traceback. It reuses the existing CPython activation hook and process setup.

The R adapter still obtains and converts reticulate's candidate configuration, translates a retained Python exception through reticulate's condition and interrupt boundary, and returns the available configuration. Requirement commits and `PythonActivated` publication remain with the active-binding write after successful activation. User-facing behavior and existing transcript expectations are unchanged; live requirement additions in sans-R sessions remain disabled.

Validation passed on macOS: `scripts/check` (core checks and smoke transcripts), the R-present activation, requirements, automatic-import, interruption, and mixed-language transcript selection before and after the change, a sans-R requirement regression, and the native subprocess activation fixture. `scripts/review-diff origin/main` reports 224 production lines added and 134 deleted, for 358 additions plus deletions.

title: Make Console own selected Python interpreter startup
description:
## Summary

Console now initializes the Python interpreter selected by reticulate, separating native startup from R interoperability as a step toward a future mode without R. Python-first cells and Python use from R reach the same retained CPython library before reticulate attaches.

## Changes

- The native owner tracks interpreter initialization separately from Console runtime setup and releases the library-state lock before interpreter execution or reentrant callbacks. Existing R FFI entry points stay in the reticulate adapter.
- Reticulate supplies the configuration and environment inputs before Python starts, preserving discovery precedence, R selection hints, and pre-initialization callbacks. It then attaches conversion, cross-language calls, and event integration.
- Interruptions while applying or serializing a fresh selection restore the captured environment inputs, including an unset or previously set `VIRTUAL_ENV`. Once CPython is running, attachment errors propagate with the selected environment retained; only temporary `PYTHONPATH` is restored. This avoids rollback and environment reapplication after interpreter startup.
- Public transcripts cover both startup orders, native initialization before attachment, once-only setup, conversion, cancellation through serialization, attachment retries after C initialization, and recovery from incompatible uv requirements.

Python remains lazy, R remains required and eagerly initialized, and interpreter-selection policy, requirement transitions, live activation, and server/worker protocols are preserved.

Local validation: the focused startup, lifecycle, selection, requirements, mixed-language, and shutdown transcript suites passed. The latest full `scripts/check` stopped in the unchanged workflow cancellation test: the nested stubborn phase returned exit code 1 instead of 143. That case passed when rerun alone. The production diff is 566 additions plus 162 deletions, 728 lines total, measured with `scripts/review-diff origin/main` with intended new files staged.

title: Move managed Python requirement transitions into the native owner
description:
Move managed Python declaration transitions and preparation orchestration into the existing native requirement owner so explicit `requirements.python`, automatic imports, and managed `reticulate::py_require()` declarations share the same decisions. This is an internal refactor with no intended user-facing behavior changes.

The native owner chooses add/remove/set transitions, handles exclusion-date rules and no-ops, and decides when to materialize or activate a candidate. It preserves lazy declarations, requirement restoration after failed preparation, and activation notification timing. Resolver-imposed interpreter constraints remain separate from retained user declarations. R field presence, ordering, attributes, encodings, history, and copy isolation stay in `src/python/requirements/r.rs`; call-local candidates do not introduce another retained manifest.

Reticulate still converts declaration arguments, performs the existing live version/package and `libpython` compatibility checks, and mutates the live environment to activate the chosen executable. The automatic-import callback remains an R-facing forwarding function. Interpreter discovery and startup, interrupt policy, and server/worker protocols are unchanged.

`scripts/check` passed, including core checks, all 967 applicable transcript executions, and source/wheel installation checks. The 154 existing requirement, automatic-resolution, and Python lifecycle executions passed before and after the change with unchanged snapshots. Three new public acceptance cases pass in direct and sandboxed modes; they cover independence from reticulate's old planner, failed-preparation restoration, no-op resolver behavior, retained version declarations, existing live validation errors, and R activation-interrupt conditions.

Production review volume from `scripts/review-diff origin/main`, after staging the new files: **596 lines changed (541 additions + 55 deletions)** across three production files, including the retained R adapter changes. The hard ceiling is 2,000.

title: Store Python requirement state as native Rust values
description:
Store the current Python requirement fields and pending activation key as native Rust values so operative requirement state no longer depends on retained R objects.

The R adapter retains field layout, attributes, string encodings, and history, and reconstructs isolated getter values. It reconstructs the pending key for the existing R identity comparison, preserving matching semantics and the point at which a successful requirement write publishes activation. There is one authoritative manifest; metadata contains no second mutable copy of its operative fields.

This is an internal representation change with no intended public behavior changes. Field presence, ordering, duplicates, missing and empty values, attributes, history, and copy isolation are preserved. Requirement transitions, interpreter selection and startup, resolver calls, compatibility checks, live activation, and automatic-import routing are unchanged. The added public regression covers attribute and encoding round trips and input/output copy isolation in direct and sandboxed modes; its expected transcript was generated against the original implementation. Existing transcript expectations are unchanged.

Validation: the 50 selected requirement and Python lifecycle cases passed before the refactor; all 51 cases, including the new regression, passed afterward. All four formatters passed. On clean commit `8c4b48bc`, `UV_CACHE_DIR=/Users/tomasz/.cache/uv scripts/check` passed in 13 minutes: core checks, 589 transcript cases (54 capability-based skips), and source/wheel installation checks. The initial default invocation hit the unchanged runner fixture's 10-second deadline while preparing a fresh uv cache; the same focused case passed in 1.2 seconds with the existing cache. No test deadlines or expectations were changed. Linux-only and unavailable optional Docker, Docker Sandbox, and external SSH cases were skipped by the harness.

Production diff measured with `scripts/review-diff origin/main`, after staging the new adapter: **492 lines** (**364 additions + 128 deletions**), including moved code, below the 2,000-line limit.

title: Decouple local Python preparation from R bootstrap
description:
## Summary

Local host Python preparation now captures direct `uv` selection independently of R discovery. Version inventory and package resolution can run before R library preparation, without a `ManagedR` value or an R, Rscript, or `ir` subprocess. Sessions still initialize R eagerly and commit the complete environment candidate only after all preparation succeeds.

## User-facing behavior

An explicit `RETICULATE_UV` executable takes precedence over `uv` on `PATH`; an invalid explicit selection fails when invoked. `RETICULATE_UV=managed` retains its existing behavior. Configurations that depend on reticulate to provide `uv` keep that R-specific fallback. SSH and prepared-target behavior is unchanged.

## Internal changes

The local path reuses the existing resolver process owner for output, cancellation, and child cleanup. Interrupts between resolver subprocesses now complete without waiting for a child that has not started. A follow-up fix marks each R, Python, and DuckDB resolver child active before publishing its interrupt handle, so signal errors reach the interrupt caller. The remote adapters, generation checks, and provisional-candidate commit owners remain in place.

The production diff is 450 additions and 226 deletions, or 676 lines total, as reported by `scripts/review-diff origin/main` after staging the new files. Relevant resolver, requirement, R fallback, startup, cancellation, and DuckDB cases passed locally. The complete `scripts/check` gate passed on the updated branch.

title: Move live managed Python activation into native requirement owner
description:
## Summary

Move live managed-Python activation into Console's native requirement owner, which already selects and prepares candidates. Explicit requirements, automatic imports, and managed `reticulate::py_require()` calls now reach the same CPython activation path.

## Behavior and ownership

Live activation still runs the selected environment's `activate_this.py`, preserves the running interpreter and its objects, updates Python and multiprocessing executables, and completes process-environment setup. Public regression cases cover activation with reticulate's former mutation helper disabled, configuration agreement, spawned children, incompatible `libpython`, Python exception reporting, requirement restoration, and R interrupts.

Reticulate still supplies candidate configuration through the existing adapter and receives the activated configuration before its requirement write publishes `PythonActivated`. The native owner compares the candidate with reticulate's existing live `libpython`, performs activation through the retained CPython library, and records the pending activation only after process setup succeeds. The current manifest, preparation flow, and server and worker protocols remain in place.

The selected requirement, automatic-resolution, and Python lifecycle suites passed before and after the change. `scripts/check --quick` and `scripts/check` passed locally on the clean PR head. The production diff is 99 additions and 67 deletions, 166 lines total, measured with `scripts/review-diff origin/main` after staging the new snapshots.

title: Unify sandbox manager retirement paths
description:
## Summary

Give the sandbox manager one concrete retirement pipeline after it adopts the root and private directory. The event loop now reports an explicit exit cause, and one manager state owns process cleanup, owner-control completion, error assembly, and directory disposition.

This removes the separate startup-failure, root-exit, owner-loss, and observation-failure completion helpers so cleanup sequencing and error policy have one owner, while preserving the order each cause requires.

## User-facing changes

- No intentional user-facing changes.
- Preserve command exit status, detached-descendant cleanup, owner-EOF behavior, and private-directory removal after successful cleanup.

## Internal changes

- Route all post-adoption completion through `ExitCause` and one `retire()` function.
- Keep observation-failure cleanup tracker-first so its final snapshot runs before root termination can reparent an unrecorded detached child.
- Keep startup cleanup success separate from the startup error so a safe private directory can still be removed.
- Preserve existing compound cleanup diagnostics.

## Validation

- `scripts/check-core`
- Eight focused public sandbox lifecycle cases covering natural root exit, owner loss, the root-exit signal race, restart, shutdown, pre-readiness manager failure, and CLI and MCP manager-crash recovery
- `scripts/check` completed the core checks, but three Python joblib and multiprocessing transcript cases could not allocate `SemLock` objects because the host POSIX semaphore namespace was exhausted. The same cases failed under `--jobs 1`; a direct host probe could allocate only eight additional semaphores.

title: Install the bundled Python evaluator through Rust
description:
## Summary

Move compile-time ownership and installation of the bundled Python evaluator from the reticulate bridge to the Rust runtime facade. This removes the embedded-R execution dependency from evaluator installation while keeping the current backend and its behavior intact.

## User-facing changes

There are no intended user-facing or transcript changes. The built-in worker still embeds R, and reticulate still owns R/Python object conversion, evaluation dispatch, managed-package hooks, output, input, interrupts, and plots.

## Internal changes

- Execute `runtime.py` through the Rust-owned CPython API while holding the GIL, using the persistent `__main__` globals and a fresh private locals dictionary to match the previous `py_run_string(local = TRUE)` bootstrap.
- Replace the R-side runtime-source callback with one installer callback while preserving direct initialization, already-initialized attachment, and initialization retry behavior.
- Document that Rust owns the evaluator source and installation boundary while reticulate continues to own the adapter lifecycle.

This change does not add a Python-only worker or change SQL ownership.

## Validation

- `scripts/check`
- Complete `client_server/python` transcript suite and focused initialization, retry, namespace, R-first initialization, and thread-release cases
- Persistent Python evaluation with locally installed CPython 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14
- Release wheel build and installed-wheel smoke test
- `R CMD check --no-manual` (`Status: OK`)
- GitHub macOS CI on the final head

title: Resolve managed Python environments directly with uv
description:
## Summary

Move managed Python environment creation out of the helper R process and into the server-owned Rust resolver. This completes the direct host-side Python resolution begun in #158 and removes reticulate and jsonlite from environment creation while keeping reticulate as the runtime conversion and evaluation backend.

## User-facing changes

- Resolve Python constraints against `uv`'s inventory, then create the selected environment with a direct `uv tool run --isolated` call.
- Preserve the stable startup `uv` selection, Python source preferences, and current managed R library across version inventory and environment creation. Recognized disabled `UV_MANAGED_PYTHON` and `UV_NO_MANAGED_PYTHON` aliases are treated as no-ops.
- Keep retained environments usable when startup sets `UV_NO_CACHE` by suppressing it only for the environment-creation command.
- Stop between resolver phases after an accepted interrupt, avoid committing an interrupted cache warmup, and preserve useful output from resolver commands that fail.

The MCP interface and Python cell transcript behavior are unchanged.

## Internal changes

- Remove the embedded `managed_python.R` program and its JSON standard-input boundary.
- Pass validated requirements as individual `--with` arguments and return the resolved interpreter through a server-created output file that is removed after use.
- Use one generation-scoped resolver lifecycle across inventory, environment creation, and Matplotlib cache warming.
- Cover version selection, startup environment propagation, interruption boundaries, cache behavior, and the reticulate-managed `uv` path through public MCP transcript tests.

## Scope

Reticulate remains the runtime conversion and evaluation backend. This does not add a Python-only worker, move SQL, change runtime threading, or expand platform support.

## Testing

- `scripts/check` on macOS, including the real reticulate-managed `uv` acceptance case

title: Wait for Python resolver exit without polling
description:
## Summary

Replace the Python resolver's 10 millisecond timed polling with a blocking lifecycle event. This removes periodic wakeups while preserving shutdown cancellation and prevents inherited resolver pipes from delaying completion after the direct `Rscript` process exits.

## User-facing changes

- Python preparation completes when the direct resolver exits, even when a descendant inherited its standard-output or standard-error pipe.
- MCP Console stops remaining members of the resolver process group before collecting output.
- Closing MCP input still cancels an in-flight resolution. Resolution retains its existing no-timeout behavior.

## Internal changes

- Wait for direct-process exit through `waitid(..., WNOWAIT)` and coordinate it with lifecycle cancellation through a blocking channel.
- Keep the resolver thread responsible for process-group termination and reaping, which avoids races with reused process-group IDs.
- Add public CLI regressions for direct-process exit with inherited pipes and bounded shutdown during Python preparation.

title: Simplify client registration and refresh website onboarding
description:
Use `--directory PATH` as the single destination option for client registration. Without it, registration uses the client's global configuration, including inside Git repositories. Use `--directory .` for the current directory. Remove `--scope` and automatic Git-root destination selection; existing `--scope` invocations now fail argument parsing.

Keep direct configuration edits, global home overrides, upfront tool exposure, launch customization, and project-entry warnings. Internal changes remove the scope enum and destination-selection branch; public acceptance cases and generated help cover the smaller interface.

Refresh the homepage and onboarding around persistent R, Python, and SQL sessions. Use `uvx` for first setup, simplify guide navigation, and consolidate platform setup. Remove the Windows experimental label while retaining MXC requirements and compatibility anchors. Keep permission examples and project-configuration trust boundaries in their owning guides.

Validated locally on macOS with 28 registration and help cases, all 21 rendered-website checks, `scripts/format`, `git diff --check`, and `scripts/check`.

title: Derive tool presentation from launch configuration
description:
## Summary

Construct the `send` schema and descriptions from captured launch configuration, independently of runtime discovery. This is the first prerequisite for a fast MCP handshake.

- Keep configured R, Python, and SQL fields stable across runtime availability and managed/bare environments. Discovered capabilities still reject unsupported calls before worker startup or replacement.
- Describe bridges, SQL ownership, and preparation conditionally. Prepared Docker/SBX targets retain read-only requirement inspection, while custom-worker prose avoids built-in runtime defaults.
- Derive placement and security prose from configuration without exposing discovered runtime paths or claiming completed probes.
- Include the actual unexpected startup response in wheel-smoke failures, without weakening the result comparison.
- Remove the Python-only schema rewrite and its unused presentation getter. Runtime discovery, preparation, initialization, lifecycle, protocols, and recording ownership are unchanged.

Public regressions compare equivalent configurations across discovered runtimes and retain explicit language filtering, requirement validation, and peer-state checks. Snapshot compaction prefers canonical execution-mode references when equivalent aliases exist.

## Intentional capability-advertising trade-off

The schema advertises capabilities Console supports, subject to explicit configuration, even when the execution host lacks a runtime. Tailoring tools to installed runtimes gives more precise guidance, but hiding an unavailable language also hides the opportunity to make it available. An advertised R field lets an agent discover that R is missing, inform the user, and request authorization to install it on the execution host. The cost is less environment-specific guidance and a possible rejected call. Advertising a capability does not authorize installation or guarantee availability.

Explicit language filtering and prepared-target restrictions remain. Runtime checks reject unavailable language calls before worker startup or replacement. Installing or configuring a missing runtime requires a new MCP server session; `control="restart"` retains the server's captured runtime selection. The decision and its limits are documented in `docs/TOOL_DESCRIPTIONS.md`, with the startup boundary linked from `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`.

This is a public interface change, not merely an internal timing refactor. Description construction no longer depends on discovery results, but server construction still performs discovery and applicable initial preparation before `initialize` and `tools/list`. Hosts with no viable runtime can still fail before advertising tools. Fast handshake remains a separate follow-up.

## Validation

- Release build and Clippy passed. The new prepared-runtime presentation regression failed against main and passed with this change; ten focused protocol/admission cases and four focused snapshot-runner regressions passed.
- On a capable macOS host, canonical handshake regeneration, the ordinary `scripts/check` gate, all 50 transcript-runner tests, and all four formatters passed. Generated snapshot changes were committed.
- The full snapshot update remains incomplete: it stopped at `cli/sandbox/test_uv::installs_a_local_wheel_into_private_storage` because uv emitted unexpected PubGrub INFO lines on stderr. It recorded 92 passing cases and 79 capability skips before stopping.
- The macOS SDK adapter regression was reproduced and now passes locally in direct and sandbox modes, together with ten schema/admission selectors (12 executions). The corresponding SSH schema expectation is aligned with the same contract.
- The new public wheel-smoke diagnostic regression was verified red/green; three focused smoke tests passed. Ubuntu CI remains under investigation: the diagnostic preserves the actual unexpected JSON response instead of reporting only the later shutdown error.

- Documentation-only update: Yamark and `git diff --check` passed. The cloud `scripts/format` run lacked Cargo/Rustfmt and Air; `scripts/check` stopped during staging because its default cache directory was read-only. No runtime source changes are introduced by the documentation commit.

## Next slice

The pre-MCP blocking path remains `run_server` policy capture and `ConsoleServer::new` client construction, including execution-host discovery and initial preparation. Moving that work behind the handshake belongs to the next PR; this change introduces no background startup or warm-worker lifecycle.

title: Speed up local validation and reuse sandbox builds
description:
New worktrees rebuilt the pinned sandbox companion, and two recovery stress tests restarted the worker for every cell. This change reduces that repeated setup and provides a smaller gate for local iteration.

Source installations and worktrees now share the pinned sandbox source and Cargo build data in the user cache. Staging locks that source through preparation, compilation, and artifact copying, and still invokes Cargo to check freshness. Application build output and staged bundles remain local to each checkout. A fresh staging directory reused the warm companion build in about one second.

For development, use a focused `scripts/test SELECTOR`, then `scripts/check --quick` for broader feedback. The quick profile retains core and ordinary transcript coverage while skipping installation checks, three extended stress cases, and real external SSH/Docker/SBX integrations. Plain `scripts/check` and CI retain the full gate. Completed transcript executions now record their mode, status, and duration beside the validation record.

Internally, silent-cell and image-omission recovery stress reuse workers through interrupt handoff. Their 512/1,024 cycles, deterministic cancellation checkpoints, and allocation limits remain intact; recorded-cell recovery still covers restarts. Focused macOS runs took about 56 and 112 seconds, compared with 224 and 457 seconds in the audited runs. The release-selection fixture also keeps uv downloads shared while isolating its concurrency budget. Console's runtime API and implementation are unchanged.

title: Move response recovery and reuse decoded image bytes
description:
Response assembly cloned the retained preview, including up to 8 MiB of encoded images, even though it consumed the response. Move that preview into its recovery owner after rendering. Cell images now decode and validate before taking the output lock and pass the decoded bytes to a small artifact-persistence method.

Public output stays unchanged: recovery remains complete until transport settlement, malformed images are validated before omission, and idle images and recording failures retain their existing response-side persistence path.

- Production: 19 added / 10 removed lines across response ownership, cell image ingestion, and transcript persistence.
- Tests: a public cancellation/recovery allocation check verifies exact image bytes, MIME type, and reuse of the original artifact; an oversized malformed-image case preserves validation before admission.
- Snapshots: two new transcripts; existing transcripts unchanged.
- Documentation: no document changes.

On macOS arm64, five runs of recovery assembly for an 8 MiB encoded image requested 16,786,994 allocation bytes before and 8,398,226 after. A complete recorded image send used approximately 14 MiB fewer allocation bytes. Its elapsed time remained around 51–52 ms; this measurement establishes an allocation reduction, not a runtime speedup.

`scripts/format` and `scripts/check` passed, including public output/recovery/transport transcripts and source/wheel installation checks. The new allocation assertion failed on the base revision. Capability-inapplicable cases were skipped by the repository runner.

title: Reduce preview allocation work
description:
Many tiny output events repeatedly copy the retained preview, and text-size checks copy image payloads they never inspect. This reduces that allocation work without changing response content or the 8 KiB text budget.

The preview batches compaction as retained text grows. Projection sizing counts text directly without constructing content blocks or cloning encoded images. Public MCP allocation regressions exercise a 100,000-event stream and a response near the image allowance while also checking the rendered output.

Incremental diff: 6 files, +294/−44; runtime files +61/−41, tests +121/−3, snapshots +110, documentation +2.

title: Bound pending worker output with an ordered tape
description:
## Summary

Unpolled worker output could grow without bound, and response boundary and newline rules were split across several server paths. This change moves server-side output ownership into one bounded ordered tape and one response assembler while retaining the existing MCP, relay, and worker protocols.

## User-facing changes

- Limit pending ordinary output to 8 MiB of combined text and direct-output bytes, 8 MiB of encoded image payloads, 64 KiB of image metadata, and 4096 output events.
- Return one bracketed truncation notice with omitted byte and event counts. Truncation does not turn an otherwise successful language evaluation into a tool error.
- Delimit output produced while idle from a newly submitted cell with `[output produced while idle]` when both regions are nonempty.
- Preserve prelude, cell, truncation, and lifecycle output exactly once when a send response is cancelled or dropped before restart claims it.
- Continue merging stdout, stderr, console output, and console diagnostics into public MCP text blocks.

## Internal changes

- Replace response checkpoints with opaque server-owned tape cuts. Completed cells drain only through their completion cut, empty polls cut the currently available output, and restart drains old-generation output from the same tape.
- Centralize text coalescing, image ordering, logical separators, notices, terminal states, and infrastructure errors in one response builder.
- Track response delivery through the JSON-RPC write so restart cannot overtake assembled output and an unclaimed response can be recovered.
- Add deterministic unit and process-boundary regressions for budgets, UTF-8 boundaries, images, terminal projections, idle preludes, completion cuts, worker failures, replacement, and response cancellation.
- Keep the flat synchronous relay as an ordered transport and worker supervisor. The relay has no response-cut or acknowledgment role and does not claim real-time ordering across independent pipes.

## Notes

This change adds no configuration file, artifact spill, ANSI interpretation, multi-session behavior, or public stdout/stderr schema.

title: Refactor sandbox launcher into reusable command builder
description:
## Summary

Refactor the macOS sandbox launcher into a reusable internal command abstraction so future long-lived workers can configure arguments, environment variables, and standard I/O before spawning without duplicating the sandbox policy or temporary-directory lifecycle. The existing `mcp-console sandbox` command now uses this abstraction.

## User-facing changes

There are no intended command-line behavior changes. `mcp-console sandbox` continues to preserve the requested program and arguments, inherit standard I/O, return the child exit status, apply the existing sandbox policy and private `TMPDIR`, and report the existing unsupported-platform error.

Executable names containing `=` remain valid because environment variables are configured on the process directly, without a shell or `/usr/bin/env`. macOS still filters `DYLD_*` variables while launching `sandbox-exec`; the abstraction documents that it does not restore them inside the sandbox.

## Internal changes

- Add `SandboxedCommand` methods for arguments, environment variables, standard I/O, synchronous status, and asynchronous spawn.
- Transfer the private temporary-directory guard to `SandboxedChild` so it remains alive for the child-process lifetime.
- Separate macOS launcher construction, spawning, waiting, and exit-code conversion while retaining the existing policy and cleanup behavior.
- Cover stable public behavior with the sandbox golden transcripts, including an executable name containing `=`, while retaining dynamic Cargo tests for host-side state and cleanup.

title: Guard workspace writes against unsafe roots
description:
MCP clients can launch Console from `/` or `HOME`, causing the workspace profile to grant broad writes. Use the read-only base for filesystem roots, home, and its ancestors, with a warning. Explicit broad grants must use absolute paths; ordinary project-relative writes remain available. If home cannot be determined, implicit grants fall back to read-only.

Use Console's home selection, including explicit `HOME` precedence on Windows, and check absent paths before granting writes. `config resolve` preserves the configured profile and write grants; the guard applies when a sandbox launches.

Share the checks across worker, resolver, and standalone sandbox policies. Check generated relative cache roots before resolving or creating their directories, and recheck relative grants before every native launch, including worker replacement. Limit the resolver-only helper export to Unix to fix the Windows Clippy failure.

Add public regressions for broad roots, aliases, absent or unset home, explicit overrides, resolver caches, configuration exports, and worker restarts. Document the permission boundary and keep repeated handshakes under canonical transcript references.

Related: [posit-dev/mcp-repl#29](https://github.com/posit-dev/mcp-repl/issues/29).

Validated on macOS with the focused sandbox, configuration, profile, and cache suites and `scripts/check`; Linux and Windows were not run locally.

title: Cover unusable Python libraries before target readiness
description:
Add a public startup regression for a selected CPython embedding library that exists but cannot be loaded. It requires rejection before MCP readiness and a failed process exit.

The case runs locally and, when their existing prepared fixtures are available, through Docker and SBX. It reuses the prepared-runtime probe harness and retirement assertions, with a shared generated result snapshot.

The public API and runtime implementation are unchanged.

title: Cover no-R SSH catalogs, input, and captured selections
description:
Add real OpenSSH acceptance in direct and native sandbox modes for Python and SQL sessions without R. The tests check a shared SQL catalog, live Python package additions, unavailable-R errors, exact input delivery, and restart with retained requirements.

The remote startup uses a fixture-owned PATH without R. Poisoned controller commands verify that runtime discovery and preparation remain on the execution host. An invalid remote `R_HOME` must fail before MCP readiness. The SSH prerequisites now describe R as required for R cells.

The public execution API and SSH protocols are unchanged; implementation changes are confined to test fixtures and documentation.

title: Validate local interpreter selection and expand no-R coverage
description:
Explicit `R_HOME` selections that lack `bin/Rscript` fail during trusted runtime discovery, before MCP readiness. Managed Python selection accepts symlinked system interpreters while retaining version filtering and preference rules.

Public transcripts cover SQL catalog retention, custom connections, input, interruption, restart, crash recovery, captured R selection, temporary-storage cleanup, Matplotlib output and cache retention, and SQL-first Python startup interruption. The no-R fixtures run on hosts with R installed and include startup with only a symlinked system Python available.

Local no-R recordings retain the Quarto document's `knitr` and `ir` front matter, including accepted Python packages. A comment and the recording guide explain that IR rendering requires R on the render host, even when the recorded session ran without R.

CI and release automation smoke-test installed wheels with R and with an isolated PATH containing Python and uv but no R. Release failures include the startup response. CI discards restored R library views with missing package targets; SQL tests retain compatible DuckDB connection settings and normalize version-dependent error wrappers. The idle Python activation test receives callback output before admitting its follow-up evaluation.

Source validation honors the selected `R_HOME` and skips R parsing when Rscript is absent. `MCP_CONSOLE_TEST_BINARY` runs transcripts against an installed executable without rebuilding the checkout.

title: Consolidate sandbox process-exit observation
description:
Centralize Darwin direct-child exit observation in `src/process_exit.rs` so worker-launcher ownership and sandbox cleanup share the same `waitid` handling. Exit status remains waitable until the owning process reaps the child. This is an internal refactor; the public sandbox CLI, process ownership, and cleanup behavior remain unchanged.

Add a sandbox dependency-direction check to `scripts/check-core`, covering shared modules and language adapters as well as the server, relay, and worker. The lexical check handles explicit paths and grouped imports while ignoring comments and string literals; relay control arguments are checked separately in literals. It runs on Python 3.8 and includes command-line regressions. The repository map now identifies the shared exit module and architecture check.

Fix timing assumptions in stdin transcripts and resolver interruption tests. Collect exact ordered stdin output, and verify that interrupted R and Python resolvers are reaped while their normal completion gate stays blocked. The R interruption transcript now waits for completion before expecting idle.

title: Make the sandbox manager the sole directory-cleanup owner after readiness
description:
## Summary

Make the sandbox manager the only directory-cleanup owner after it reports readiness. The host owner now relinquishes its guard without retaining a raw recovery path, while manager-failure fallback remains responsible only for bounded process cleanup.

The manager's adopted directory guard now preserves on unexpected unwind and arms removal only after cleanup proves that the directory is unused. This keeps normal cleanup unchanged while preventing a manager panic from removing a directory whose process lifetime has not been fully accounted for.

## User-facing changes

- A sandbox-manager panic after readiness preserves the private temporary directory while the launcher or server performs fallback process cleanup.
- Normal cleanup still removes the directory after the manager successfully retires the sandbox lifetime.
- A failed manager may intentionally leave a private temporary directory behind when it cannot prove that the directory is unused.

## Internal changes

- Remove the owner's post-readiness recovery path and direct directory removal.
- Make adopted manager guards preserve by default, with explicit removal on each successful manager cleanup path.
- Add a deterministic macOS CLI transcript that injects tracker-thread creation failure and verifies process cleanup and directory preservation.
- Synchronize the architecture, supervision, relay, and contributor documentation with the ownership boundary.

## Testing

- `scripts/format`
- `scripts/check`
- `scripts/check-core`
- `scripts/test cli/sandbox_crash`
- `scripts/test client_server/sandbox_crash`
- `scripts/test client_server/sandbox_startup`
- `scripts/test client_server/r::restart_skips_direct_stdin_boundary_callback`

## Limitations

Owner-side fallback can reconstruct only descendants still reachable from the pinned root's current ancestry. A descendant that detached before the manager failed remains outside that fallback guarantee.

title: Fix Windows validation follow-ups and update cobox
description:
Advance cobox to `bad761ee97eb54caf302d6d4261ef494f686bf12` from t-kalinowski/cobox#59 so inherited Command Prompt metadata such as `=ExitCode` no longer prevents sandbox launches. Add a public regression that runs through real CMD, update the pinned schema link, and document inherited versus explicitly configured environment names. The release/toolchain and private wire contract are unchanged.

Also address the failures found during Windows validation of #662:

- Normalize website path separators before classifying repository links. R README links remain in the local package site; source/template links become valid GitHub URLs. Test package, guide, template, and source links at both directory depths, including queries and fragments.
